## Appendix A Proofs

### A.1 Proof for Theorem 2.1

#### Proof.

For simplicity, we assume there is no tie and let $\pi$ be a permutation such that

$$ \eta_{\pi(1)}\geq\eta_{\pi(2)}\geq\cdots\geq\eta_{\pi(p)}. $$

Define $M_{j}=r_{j}\eta_{j}$ with $\eta_{j}\geq 0$ . Then for any $t>0$ ,

$$ \{j:M_{j}>t\}=\{j:r_{j}=1,\ \eta_{j}>t\},\qquad\{j:M_{j}<-t\}=\{j:r_{j}=-1,\ \eta_{j}>t\}. $$

Hence the SeqStep FDP estimate can be written as

$$ \widehat{\mathrm{FDP}}(t)=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{p}\mathbf{1}\{r_{j}=-1,\ \eta_{j}>t\}}{\sum_{j=1}^{p}\mathbf{1}\{r_{j}=1,\ \eta_{j}>t\}\ \vee\ 1}. $$

Next, let $\eta_{(1)}\geq\cdots\geq\eta_{(p)}$ denote the order statistics so that $\eta_{(k)}=\eta_{\pi(k)}$ , and define the top- $k$ prefix set

$$ A_{k}:=\{\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(k)\}. $$

Fix $k\in\{0,1,\ldots,p\}$ and choose any threshold $t$ such that

$$ \eta_{(k)}>t\geq\eta_{(k+1)}, $$

with the convention $\eta_{(0)}:=+\infty$ and $\eta_{(p+1)}:=-\infty$ . Then $\{j:\eta_{j}>t\}=A_{k}$ . Plugging this into (A.1) yields

$$ \widehat{\mathrm{FDP}}(t)=\frac{\sum_{j\in A_{k}}\mathbf{1}\{r_{j}=-1\}}{\sum_{j\in A_{k}}\mathbf{1}\{r_{j}=1\}\ \vee\ 1}=:\widehat{\mathrm{FDP}}[k], $$

which is exactly the two-stage estimated FDP after examining $k$ features.

Note that the map $t\mapsto\widehat{\mathrm{FDP}}(t)$ is a step function that is constant on each interval $(\eta_{(k+1)},\eta_{(k)}]$ and equals $\widehat{\mathrm{FDP}}[k]$ there. Therefore,

$$ \tau_{q}:=\min\{t>0:\widehat{\mathrm{FDP}}(t)\leq q\} $$

is attained on the interval corresponding to the largest index $\widehat{k}$ such that $\widehat{\mathrm{FDP}}[\widehat{k}]\leq q$ , i.e., the two-stage stopping index.

Finally, the SeqStep selection set is

$$ \widehat{S}_{\mathrm{SeqStep}}=\{j:M_{j}>\tau_{q}\}=\{j:r_{j}=1,\ \eta_{j}>\tau_{q}\}=\{j\in A_{\widehat{k}}:r_{j}=1\}, $$

which matches the two-stage discoveries (the correct guesses among the examined prefix). This proves the claimed equivalence. ∎

### A.2 Proof for Proposition 2.1

First, we introduce a lemma demonstrating the weak dependence for mirror statistic from Assumption 2.2 and the rest of the proof largely follows Dai et al. (2023b).

#### Lemma A.1.

[Assumption 2 in Dai et al. (2023b)] The mirror statistic $M_{j}$ ’s are continuous random variables and there exist constant $c$ and $\alpha\in(0,2)$ such that

$$ \Var\left(\sum_{j\in S_{0}}\mathbbm{1}(M_{j}>t)\right)\leq cp_{0}^{\alpha},\quad\forall t\in\mathbb{R},\quad\text{where }p_{0}=|S_{0}|. $$

For the ease of presentation, we introduce the following notations. For any $t\in\mathbb{R}$ , denote

$$ \hat{G}_{p}^{0}(t)=\frac{1}{p_{0}}\sum_{j\in S_{0}}1(M_{j}>t),\quad G_{p}^{0}(t)=\frac{1}{p_{0}}\sum_{j\in S_{0}}\mathbb{P}(M_{j}>t), $$

$$ \hat{G}_{p}^{1}(t)=\frac{1}{p_{1}}\sum_{j\in S_{1}}1(M_{j}>t),\quad\hat{V}_{p}(t)=\frac{1}{p_{0}}\sum_{j\in S_{0}}1(M_{j}<-t). $$

Let $r_{p}=p_{1}/p_{0}$ . In addition, denote

$$ \text{FDP}_{p}(t)=\frac{\hat{G}_{p}^{0}(t)}{\hat{G}_{p}^{0}(t)+r_{p}\hat{G}_{p}^{1}(t)},\quad\text{FDP}_{p}(t)=\frac{G_{p}^{0}(t)}{G_{p}^{0}(t)+r_{p}\hat{G}_{p}^{1}(t)}. $$

We also know that $\widehat{\text{FDP}}$ can be written as

$$ \widehat{\text{FDP}}=\frac{\hat{V}_{p}^{0}(t)}{\hat{G}_{p}^{0}(t)+r_{p}\hat{G}_{p}^{1}(t)}. $$

The rest of the proof is essentially to show that $\widehat{\text{FDP}}$ approximates FDP fairly well when $p\to\infty$ . Consequently, controlling $\widehat{\text{FDP}}$ generalizes controlling FDP.

#### Lemma A.2.

Under Lemma A.1, and assuming $p_{0}\to\infty$ as $p\to\infty$ , we have, in probability,

$$ \sup_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\left|\hat{G}_{p}^{0}(t)-G_{p}^{0}(t)\right|\to 0,\quad\sup_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\left|\hat{V}_{p}(t)-G_{p}^{0}(t)\right|\to 0. $$

Proof of Lemma A.1.

Since $\mathbbm{1}(M_{j}>t)$ is a random bounded function of the summary statistics $s_{j}$ taking value between $-1$ and $1$ . This lemma is a direct consequence of Assumption 2.2.

Proof of Lemma A.2. For any $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ , denote $-\infty=\alpha_{0}^{p}<\alpha_{1}^{p}<\cdots<\alpha_{N_{\epsilon}}^{p}=\infty$ with $N_{\epsilon}=\lceil 2/\epsilon\rceil$ , such that $G_{p}^{0}(\alpha_{k-1}^{p})-G_{p}^{0}(\alpha_{k}^{p})\leq\epsilon/2$ for $k=1,\dots,N_{\epsilon}$ . By Lemma A.1, such a sequence $\{\alpha_{k}^{p}\}$ exists since $G_{p}^{0}(t)$ is a continuous function for $t\in\mathbb{R}$ . We have

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\left|\hat{G}_{p}^{0}(t)-G_{p}^{0}(t)\right|>\epsilon\right)\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{N_{\epsilon}}\sup_{t\in[\alpha_{k-1}^{p},\alpha_{k}^{p}]}\left|\hat{G}_{p}^{0}(t)-G_{p}^{0}(t)\right|>\epsilon\right), $$

$$ \leq\sum_{k=1}^{N_{\epsilon}}\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{t\in[\alpha_{k-1}^{p},\alpha_{k}^{p}]}\left|\hat{G}_{p}^{0}(t)-G_{p}^{0}(t)\right|>\epsilon\right). $$

We note that both $\hat{G}_{p}^{0}(t)$ and $G_{p}^{0}(t)$ are monotonically decreasing. Therefore, $\forall k\in\{1,\dots,N_{\epsilon}\}$ , we have

$$ \sup_{t\in[\alpha_{k-1}^{p},\alpha_{k}^{p}]}\left|\hat{G}_{p}^{0}(t)-G_{p}^{0}(t)\right|\leq\left|\hat{G}_{p}^{0}(\alpha_{k-1}^{p})-G_{p}^{0}(\alpha_{k-1}^{p})\right|+\epsilon/2. $$

By Equation (A.2), Lemma A.1, and the Chebyshev’s inequality, it follows that

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\left|\hat{G}_{p}^{0}(t)-G_{p}^{0}(t)\right|>\epsilon\right)\leq\sum_{k=1}^{N_{\epsilon}}\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\hat{G}_{p}^{0}(\alpha_{k-1}^{p})-G_{p}^{0}(\alpha_{k-1}^{p})\right|>\frac{\epsilon}{2}\right)\leq\frac{4cN_{\epsilon}}{p_{0}^{2}\epsilon^{2}}\to 0,\quad\text{as }p\to\infty. $$

Similarly, we can show that

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\left(\hat{G}_{p}^{0}(t)-G_{p}^{0}(t)\right)<-\epsilon\right)\leq\sum_{k=1}^{N_{\epsilon}}\mathbb{P}\left(\hat{G}_{p}^{0}(\alpha_{k}^{p})-G_{p}^{0}(\alpha_{k}^{p})<-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\right)\leq\frac{4cN_{\epsilon}}{p_{0}^{2}\epsilon^{2}}\to 0,\quad\text{as }p\to\infty. $$

This concludes the proof of the first claim in Lemma A.2. The second claim follows similarly using the symmetric property of the mirror statistic $M_{j}$ for $j\in S_{0}$ .

Proof of Proposition 2.1. We first show that for any $\epsilon\in(0,q)$ , we have

$$ \mathbb{P}(\tau_{q}\leq t_{q-\epsilon})\geq 1-\epsilon, $$

in which $t_{q-\epsilon}>0$ satisfying $\mathbb{P}(\text{FDP}_{p}(t_{q-\epsilon})\leq q-\epsilon)\to 1$ . Since the variances of the mirror statistics are upper bounded and also bounded away from 0, by Lemma A.2, we have

$$ \sup_{0<t\leq c}\left|\text{FDP}_{p}^{+}(t)-\text{FDP}_{p}(t)\right|\to 0 $$

for any constant $c>0$ . By the definition of $\tau_{q}$ , i.e., $\tau_{q}=\inf\{t>0:\text{FDP}_{p}(t)\leq q\}$ , we have

$$ \mathbb{P}(\tau_{q}\leq t_{q-\epsilon})\geq\mathbb{P}(\text{FDP}_{p}^{+}(t_{q-\epsilon})\leq q)\geq\mathbb{P}(|\text{FDP}_{p}^{+}(t_{q-\epsilon})-\text{FDP}_{p}(t_{q-\epsilon})|\leq\epsilon,\,\text{FDP}_{p}(t_{q-\epsilon})\leq q-\epsilon)\geq 1-\epsilon $$

for $p$ large enough. Conditioning on the event $\tau_{q}\leq t_{q-\epsilon}$ , we have

$$ \limsup_{p\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\text{FDP}_{p}(\tau_{q})\right]\leq\limsup_{p\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\text{FDP}_{p}(\tau_{q})\mid\tau_{q}\leq t_{q-\epsilon}\right]\mathbb{P}(\tau_{q}\leq t_{q-\epsilon})+\epsilon $$

$$ \leq\limsup_{p\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\text{FDP}_{p}(\tau_{q})-\text{FDP}_{p}(t_{q-\epsilon})\right|\mid\tau_{q}\leq t_{q-\epsilon}\right]\mathbb{P}(\tau_{q}\leq t_{q-\epsilon}) $$

$$ +\limsup_{p\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\text{FDP}_{p}^{+}(t_{q-\epsilon})-\text{FDP}_{p}(t_{q-\epsilon})\right|\mid\tau_{q}\leq t_{q-\epsilon}\right]\mathbb{P}(\tau_{q}\leq t_{q-\epsilon})+\epsilon $$

$$ \leq\limsup_{p\to\infty}\sup_{0<t\leq t_{q-\epsilon}}\left|\text{FDP}_{p}^{+}(t)-\text{FDP}_{p}(t)\right| $$

$$ +\limsup_{p\to\infty}\sup_{0<t\leq t_{q-\epsilon}}\left|\text{FDP}_{p}^{+}(t)-\text{FDP}_{p}(t)\right| $$

$$ +\limsup_{p\to\infty}\text{FDP}_{p}(t_{q-\epsilon})+\epsilon. $$

The first two terms are 0 based on Lemma A.2 and the dominated convergence theorem. For the third term, we have $\text{FDP}_{p}(\tau_{q})\leq q$ by the definition of $\tau_{q}$ . This concludes the proof of Proposition 2.1. ∎

### A.3 Proof for Proposition 2.2

#### Theorem A.1 (Doukhan and Neumann (2007)).

Suppose that $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ are mean-zero random variables taking values in $[-1,1]$ such that

$$ \mathrm{Var}(\bar{X}_{n})\leq C_{0}n $$

for a constant $C_{0}>0$ . Let $L_{1},L_{2}<\infty$ be constants such that for any $i\leq j$ ,

$$ \bigl|\mathrm{Cov}(X_{i},X_{j})\bigr|\leq 4\,\varphi(j-i), $$

where $\{\varphi(k)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a nonincreasing sequence satisfying

$$ \sum_{s=0}^{\infty}(s+1)^{k}\,\varphi(s)\leq L_{1}L_{2}^{k}\,k!\qquad\text{for all }k\geq 0. $$

Then for all $t\in(0,1)$ , there exists a universal constant $C_{1}>0$ only depending on $C_{0},L_{1},L_{2}$ such that

$$ \mathbb{P}(\bar{X}_{n}\geq t)\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{C_{0}n+C_{1}t^{7/4}n^{7/4}}\right)\leq\exp\!\left(-C^{\prime}t^{2}n^{1/4}\right), $$

where $C^{\prime}$ is a universal constant only depending on $C_{0},L_{1},L_{2}$ .

If we take $\varphi(s)=c\rho^{s}$ , this yields the following corollary.

#### Corollary A.1 (Spector and Fithian (2022)).

Suppose that $Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{p}$ are mean-zero random variables taking values in $[-1,1]$ . Suppose that for some $C\geq 0$ and $\rho\in(0,1)$ , the sequence satisfies

$$ \bigl|\mathrm{Cov}(Z_{i},Z_{j})\bigr|\leq C\rho^{|i-j|}. $$

Then there exists a universal constant $C^{\prime}$ depending only on $C$ and $\rho$ such that

$$ \mathbb{P}(\bar{Z}_{p}\geq t)\leq\exp\!\bigl(-C^{\prime}t^{2}p^{1/4}\bigr). $$

Furthermore, let $\pi:[p]\to[p]$ be any permutation. For $m\leq p$ , define

$$ \bar{Z}^{(\pi)}_{m}:=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}Z_{\pi(i)} $$

to be the sample mean of the first $m$ random variables after permuting $(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{p})$ according to $\pi$ . Then for any $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $t\geq 0$ ,

$$ \sup_{\pi\in S_{p}}\;\mathbb{P}\!\left(\max_{k\leq m\leq p}\bigl|\bar{Z}^{(\pi)}_{m}\bigr|\geq t\right)\leq p\,\exp\!\bigl(-C^{\prime}t^{2}k^{1/4}\bigr), $$

where $S_{p}$ is the symmetric group.

#### Proof.

The proof of (C.2) follows an observation of Doukhan and Neumann (2007), where we note $\varphi(s)=C\exp(-as)$ for $a=-\log(\rho)$ . Then

$$ \sum_{s=0}^{\infty}(s+1)^{k}\exp(-as)\leq\sum_{s=0}^{\infty}\prod_{i=1}^{k}(s+i)\exp(-as)=\left.\frac{d^{k}}{dp^{k}}\!\left(\frac{1}{1-p}\right)\right|_{p=\exp(-a)}=k!\,\frac{1}{\bigl(1-\exp(-a)\bigr)^{k}}. $$

As a result,

$$ \sum_{s=0}^{\infty}(s+1)^{k}\varphi(s)\leq C\left(\frac{1}{1-\exp(-a)}\right)^{k}k!, $$

so we take $L_{1}=\bigl(1-\exp(-a)\bigr)^{-1}$ and $L_{2}=C$ . Lastly, we observe that another geometric series argument yields

$$ \mathrm{Var}(\bar{Z}_{p})=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{p}\mathrm{Cov}(Z_{i},Z_{j})\leq\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{p}C\rho^{|i-j|}\leq pC\,\frac{2}{1-\rho}. $$

Thus, we take $C_{0}=\frac{2C}{1-\rho}$ and apply Theorem C.1, which yields the first result. To prove (C.3), the main idea is that we can apply (C.2) to each sample mean $\bigl|\bar{Z}^{(\pi)}_{m}\bigr|$ , at which point (C.3) follows from a union bound.

To prove this, note that if we rearrange $(Z_{\pi(1)},\ldots,Z_{\pi(m)})$ into their “original order,” then these variables satisfy the condition in (C.1). Formally, let $A=\{\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(m)\}$ and let $\nu:A\to A$ be the permutation such that $\nu(\pi(i))>\nu(\pi(j))$ if and only if $i>j$ , for $i,j\in[m]$ . Then define $Y_{i}=Z_{\nu(\pi(i))}$ for $i\in[m]$ , and note that

$$ \bigl|\mathrm{Cov}(Y_{i},Y_{j})\bigr|=\bigl|\mathrm{Cov}(Z_{\nu(\pi(i))},Z_{\nu(\pi(j))})\bigr|\leq C\rho^{|\nu(\pi(i))-\nu(\pi(j))|}\leq C\rho^{|i-j|}, $$

where in the last step, $|i-j|\leq|\nu(\pi(i))-\nu(\pi(j))|$ follows by construction of $\nu$ . Since $\bar{Y}_{m}=\bar{Z}^{(\pi)}_{m}$ by construction, this means we may apply (C.2) to $\bar{Z}^{(\pi)}_{m}$ for each $m$ .

Thus, by (C.2), for any $\pi\in S_{p}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}\!\left(\max_{k\leq m\leq p}\bigl|\bar{Z}^{(\pi)}_{m}\bigr|\geq t\right)\leq\sum_{m=k}^{p}\mathbb{P}\!\left(\bigl|\bar{Z}^{(\pi)}_{m}\bigr|\geq t\right)\leq\sum_{m=k}^{p}\exp\!\bigl(-C^{\prime}t^{2}m^{1/4}\bigr)\leq p\,\exp\!\bigl(-C^{\prime}t^{2}k^{1/4}\bigr). $$

This completes the proof. ∎

#### Proof.

Fix $q\in(0,1)$ and $\epsilon>0$ . Throughout, we condition on the first half of data $D^{(1)}$ and view all random quantities from the second half as conditionally independent draws given $D^{(1)}$ . For each feature $j$ , let $(s_{j}^{(2)},\tilde{s}_{j}^{(2)})$ denote its mirrored pair from the second half, and write the corresponding label variable as

$$ r_{j}=\psi_{j}(s_{j}^{(2)},\tilde{s}_{j}^{(2)},D^{(1)})\in\{\pm 1\}, $$

where $\psi_{j}$ is a measurable function that outputs the mirror sign. By construction, $r_{j}$ depends only on $(s_{j}^{(2)},\tilde{s}_{j}^{(2)})$ and the conditioning information $D^{(1)}$ .

Let $\sigma=\sigma(D^{(1)})$ be the permutation in Assumption 2.3, so that features are ordered according to the ranking scores $\eta_{j}$ and Algorithm 1 examines $\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(p)$ . For each $k$ , define the empirical quantities

$$ \widehat{X}_{k}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbbm{1}\{r_{\sigma(i)}=-1\},\qquad\widehat{Y}_{k}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbbm{1}\{r_{\sigma(i)}=1\},\qquad\widehat{\text{FDP}}[k]=\frac{\widehat{X}_{k}}{\widehat{Y}_{k}\vee k^{-1}}, $$

and their conditional expectations

$$ \widetilde{X}_{k}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbbm{P}(r_{\sigma(i)}=-1\mid D^{(1)}),\qquad\widetilde{Y}_{k}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbbm{P}(r_{\sigma(i)}=1\mid D^{(1)}),\qquad\widetilde{\text{FDP}}[k]=\frac{\widetilde{X}_{k}}{\widetilde{Y}_{k}}. $$

Because each optimal guess chooses the label with higher posterior probability under its own conditional distribution, we have $\mathbbm{P}(r_{j}=1\mid D^{(1)})\geq 1/2$ and hence $\widetilde{Y}_{k}\geq 1/2$ for all $k$ .

Since $r_{j}$ is a bounded measurable function of $(s_{j}^{(2)},\tilde{s}_{j}^{(2)},D^{(1)})$ , the data-processing property of maximal correlation Witsenhausen (1975) implies

$$ \rho_{\max}\!\left(r_{\sigma(i)},r_{\sigma(j)}\mid D^{(1)}\right)\leq\rho_{\max}\!\left(\,\left(s_{\sigma(i)}^{(2)},\tilde{s}_{\sigma(i)}^{(2)}\right),\,\left(s_{\sigma(j)}^{(2)},\tilde{s}_{\sigma(j)}^{(2)}\right)\mid D^{(1)}\right)=\Gamma_{ij}, $$

Define $Z_{i}=\mathbbm{1}\{r_{\sigma(i)}=\pm 1\}-\mathbbm{P}\{r_{\sigma(i)}=\pm 1\}\in[-1,1]$ , we also have $\rho_{\max}(Z_{i},Z_{j}\mid D^{(1)})\leq\Gamma_{ij}$ . Applying Corollary A.1 and Assumption 2.3, we have

$$ \mathbbm{P}\!\left(|\widehat{X}_{k}-\widetilde{X}_{k}|\geq t\mid D^{(1)}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-C^{\prime}t^{2}k^{1/4}\right),\qquad\mathbbm{P}\!\left(|\widehat{Y}_{k}-\widetilde{Y}_{k}|\geq t\mid D^{(1)}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-C^{\prime}t^{2}k^{1/4}\right), $$

for some constant $c=c(\alpha,C)>0$ . A union bound over $k\in[k_{0},p]$ yields

$$ \mathbbm{P}\!\left(\max_{k_{0}\leq k\leq p}\bigl|\widehat{X}_{k}-\widetilde{X}_{k}\bigr|\geq t\mid D^{(1)}\right)\leq 2p\,\exp\left(-C^{\prime}t^{2}k_{0}^{1/4}\right), $$

and similarly for $\widehat{Y}_{k}$ . Taking $k_{0}\asymp p$ ensures that these probabilities vanish, and thus

$$ \max_{k_{0}\leq k\leq p}|\widehat{X}_{k}-\widetilde{X}_{k}|=o_{\mathbbm{P}}(1),\qquad\max_{k_{0}\leq k\leq p}|\widehat{Y}_{k}-\widetilde{Y}_{k}|=o_{\mathbbm{P}}(1),\qquad\max_{k_{0}\leq k\leq p}|\widehat{\text{FDP}}[k]-\widetilde{\text{FDP}}[k]|=o_{\mathbbm{P}}(1), $$

where the last relation follows from $\widetilde{Y}_{k}\geq 1/2$ .

Let $(\psi_{j}^{\star},\eta_{j}^{\star})$ denote the optimal guess and its ranking rule, and define $r_{j}^{\star}=\psi_{j}^{\star}(s_{j}^{(2)},\tilde{s}_{j}^{(2)},D^{(1)})$ . By Bayes optimality,

$$ \mathbbm{P}(r_{j}^{\star}=-1\mid D^{(1)})\leq\mathbbm{P}(r_{j}=-1\mid D^{(1)}),\qquad\mathbbm{P}(r_{j}^{\star}=1\mid D^{(1)})\geq\mathbbm{P}(r_{j}=1\mid D^{(1)}), $$

for every competing $(\psi_{j},\eta_{j})$ . Therefore, for any examined prefix $A_{k}=\{\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(k)\}$ determined by a competitor’s order,

$$ \widetilde{X}_{k}^{\star}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j\in A_{k}}\mathbbm{P}(r_{j}^{\star}=-1\mid D^{(1)})\leq\widetilde{X}_{k},\qquad\widetilde{Y}_{k}^{\star}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j\in A_{k}}\mathbbm{P}(r_{j}^{\star}=1\mid D^{(1)})\geq\widetilde{Y}_{k}, $$

which implies $\widetilde{\text{FDP}}^{\star}[k]\leq\widetilde{\text{FDP}}[k]$ for all $k$ on the same prefix.

Fix $\zeta\in(0,1)$ and suppose $\beta(M,q)>\zeta$ . Then the competing procedure at level $q$ achieves at least $\zeta p_{1}$ true discoveries, so its stopping index $\hat{k}$ satisfies $\hat{k}\geq\zeta p_{1}\geq\zeta\gamma p$ . On the event where the uniform concentration bounds above hold for all $k\geq k_{0}=\zeta\gamma p$ , the stopping rule guarantees $\widehat{\text{FDP}}[\hat{k}]\leq q$ , hence $\widetilde{\text{FDP}}[\hat{k}]\leq q+o_{\mathbbm{P}}(1)$ . By local optimality, $\widetilde{\text{FDP}}^{\star}[\hat{k}]\leq\widetilde{\text{FDP}}[\hat{k}]\leq q+o_{\mathbbm{P}}(1)$ , and the same concentration transfer yields $\widehat{\text{FDP}}^{\star}[\hat{k}]\leq q+\epsilon$ for all large $p$ . Therefore the optimal procedure at nominal level $q+\epsilon$ will not stop before $\hat{k}$ , that is, $\hat{k}^{\star}(q+\epsilon)\geq\hat{k}$ with probability approaching one.

Because $\hat{k}^{\star}(q+\epsilon)\geq\hat{k}$ and, for every feature, the optimal guess has conditionally no smaller correctness probability than any competitor, the number of true discoveries among the first $\hat{k}$ inspected features under the optimal rule is asymptotically no smaller. Dividing by $p_{1}$ yields

$$ \beta(M^{\star},q+\epsilon)\geq\beta(M,q)-o_{\mathbbm{P}}(1), $$

and taking $\epsilon\downarrow 0$ completes the argument:

$$ \underset{0<\epsilon<1-q}{\sup}\liminf_{p\to\infty}\{\beta(M^{\star},q+\epsilon)-\beta(M,q)\}\geq 0. $$

## Appendix B Sampling Details for Spike-and-slab Prior

In this section, we will provide details in sampling from the posterior distribution for computing Bayes-optimal mirror statistics.

### B.1 Spike-and-slab Gibbs update rules for linear model

Suppose we have the following hierarchical model,

$$ \displaystyle y_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(x_{i}\beta,\sigma^{2}), \displaystyle\beta_{j}\sim(1-\pi)\delta_{0}+\pi\mathcal{N}(\mu,\tau^{2}), \displaystyle\pi_{j}\sim\text{ Bern }(\theta), \displaystyle\sigma^{2}\sim\text{ InvGamma }(a_{1},a_{2}), \displaystyle\tau^{2}\sim\text{ InvGamma }(b_{1},b_{2}), \displaystyle\theta\sim\text{ Beta }(A,B), \displaystyle\mu\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{0},\tau_{0}^{2}). $$

Each iteration consists of regression update and hyper-parameters update.

- • Update $\pi_{j}$ In regression update step, we update each feature $j$ randomly and once at a time, so it’s essentially the same as in the 1d regression problem. $\displaystyle\frac{P(\pi_{j}=0\mid\cdot)}{P(\pi_{j}=1\mid\cdot)}$ $\displaystyle=\frac{p_{0}}{1-p_{0}}\times\frac{P(y\mid X,\pi_{j}=0)}{P(y\mid X,\pi_{j}=1)}$ (B.1) $\displaystyle=\frac{p_{0}}{1-p_{0}}\times\text{det}(Q)^{1/2}\exp(-\frac{\tau^{2}}{2\sigma^{4}}(y-\mu)^{T}XQX^{T}(y-\mu))$ (B.2) $\displaystyle\quad\times\exp(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}||y||^{2}+\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}||y-\mu||^{2}),$ (B.3) where $Q=Q_{j}=1+\frac{\tau^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}||x_{j}||^{2}$ is a scalar and we denote the residual $r_{i}:=y_{i}-\sum_{l\neq j}x_{il}\beta_{l}$ , which satisfies

$$ r_{i}:=y_{i}-\sum_{l\neq j}x_{il}\beta_{l}=x_{ij}\beta_{j}+\epsilon_{i}. $$

- • Update $\beta_{j}$ When the other features except $j$ are fixed, consider the model $r_{i}=x_{ij}\beta_{j}+\epsilon_{i}$ .

$$ \beta_{j}\mid\mathbf{r},\pi_{j},\tau^{2},\sigma^{2}\sim\begin{cases}\delta_{0}&\text{if }\pi_{j}=0\\[10.0pt] \mathcal{N}\left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}x_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{2}+\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}},\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{2}+\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}}\right)&\text{if }\pi_{j}=1\end{cases} $$

- • Update Hyper-parameters If the problem is one dimensional, we have the following update rules, $\displaystyle\theta\mid\cdot=\theta\mid\pi\sim\text{ Beta }(A+\pi,B+1-\pi),$ $\displaystyle\tau^{2}\mid\beta,\mu,\pi=1\sim\text{ InvGamma }(b_{1}+\frac{1}{2},b_{2}+\frac{(\beta-\mu)^{2}}{2}),$ $\displaystyle\tau^{2}\mid\beta,\mu,\pi=0\sim\text{ InvGamma }(b_{1},b_{2}),$ $\displaystyle\mu\mid\beta,\tau^{2},\pi=1\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{\frac{\mu_{0}}{\tau_{0}^{2}}+\frac{\beta}{\tau^{2}}}{\frac{1}{\tau_{0}^{2}}+\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}},\frac{1}{\frac{1}{\tau_{0}^{2}}+\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}}\right),$ $\displaystyle\mu\mid\beta,\tau^{2},\pi=0\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{0},\tau^{2}_{0}),$ $\displaystyle\sigma^{2}\mid y,\beta\sim\text{ InvGamma }(a_{1}+\frac{n}{2},a_{2}+\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_{i}-x_{i}\beta)^{2}}{2}).$ Now in general case, we have $\displaystyle\theta\mid\cdot=\theta\mid\pi\sim\text{ Beta }(A+\sum_{j}\pi_{j},B+\sum_{j}1-\pi_{j}),$ $\displaystyle\tau^{2}\mid\beta,\mu,\pi\sim\text{ InvGamma }(b_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}\pi_{j},b_{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}\pi_{j}(\beta_{j}-\mu)^{2})\quad,$ $\displaystyle\mu\mid\beta,\tau^{2},\pi=1\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{\frac{\mu_{0}}{\tau_{0}^{2}}+\frac{\sum_{j}\beta_{j}}{\tau^{2}}}{\frac{1}{\tau_{0}^{2}}+\frac{p}{\tau^{2}}},\frac{1}{\frac{1}{\tau_{0}^{2}}+\frac{p}{\tau^{2}}}\right),$ $\displaystyle\sigma^{2}\mid y,\beta\sim\text{ InvGamma }(a_{1}+\frac{n}{2},a_{2}+\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_{i}-x_{i}\beta)^{2}}{2}).$

### B.2 Spike-and-slab update rules for logistic model

Deriving scalable sampling methods for logistic model has been actively studied in the statistical literature Ray and Szabó (2022); Biswas et al. (2022); Barndorff-Nielsen et al. (1982); Biane et al. (2001); Polson et al. (2013). However, the sampling for Spike-and-Slab logistic model is much more trickier. The approach we use follows from the $t$ -distribution approximation for the logistic distribution in O’brien and Dunson (2004); Narisetty et al. (2019). We can approximate $\text{Logistic}(x_{i}^{T}\bm{\beta},1)$ with $x_{i}^{T}\bm{\beta}+wt_{\nu}$ , where $t_{\nu}$ denotes a t-distribution with $\nu$ degrees of freedom and $w$ is a multiplicative factor. The choice of the constants $\nu=7.3$ and $w^{2}=\frac{\pi^{2}(\nu-2)}{3\nu}$ were recommended by O’brien and Dunson (2004). This allows us to re-write the Spike-and-Slab logistic model as

$$ \displaystyle z_{j} \displaystyle\overset{iid}{\sim}\text{Bernoulli}(\theta_{j}), \displaystyle\beta_{j}\mid z_{j} \displaystyle\overset{ind}{\sim}(1-z_{j})\delta_{0}+z_{j}\mathcal{N}(\mu,\tau^{2}), \displaystyle\widetilde{\sigma}^{2} \displaystyle\overset{iid}{\sim}\text{InvGamma}(\frac{\nu}{2},\frac{w^{2}\nu}{2}), \displaystyle\widetilde{y}_{i}\mid\bm{\beta},\widetilde{\sigma}^{2} \displaystyle\overset{ind}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(x_{i}^{T}\bm{\beta},\widetilde{\sigma}^{2}), \displaystyle y_{i} \displaystyle=\mathbbm{1}(\widetilde{y}_{i}>0). $$

Thus it reduces to sample from the spike-and-slab linear model discussed in the previous sub-section.
