$$ M_{\rho}(v,t)=\min_{x\in\mathbbm{R}}\left\{\rho(x)+\frac{1}{2t}(x-v)^{2}\right\}. $$

Proof of Lemma A.1. The proof heavily relies on Thrampoulidis et al., (2018) and Salehi et al., (2019), in which the key technical tool is the Convex Gaussian Min-max Theorem(CGMT). We introduce a new variable $u=X\beta$ and rewrite the optimization problem (11) as

$$ \min_{\beta\in\mathbbm{R}^{p},u\in\mathbbm{R}^{n}}\frac{1}{n}1^{\intercal}\rho(u)-\frac{1}{n}y^{\intercal}u\ \ \ \ s.t.\ \ \ \ u=X\beta. $$

Based on the method of Lagrange multipliers, the above optimization problem is equivalent to a min-max problem specified as below,

$$ (\text{PO})\ \ \ \min_{\beta\in\mathbbm{R}^{p},u\in\mathbbm{R}^{n}}\max_{v\in\mathbbm{R}^{n}}\frac{1}{n}1^{\intercal}\rho(u)-\frac{1}{n}y^{\intercal}u+\frac{1}{n}v^{\intercal}(u-X\beta). $$

We refer to this min-max optimization problem as the primary optimization (PO) problem henceforth.

We proceed to associate the PO with an auxiliary optimization (AO) problem using CGMT. Similar as in Salehi et al., (2019), We decompose $\beta=P\beta+P^{\perp}\beta$ , in which $P$ is the projection operator projecting onto the column space spanned by $\beta^{\star}$ , and rewrite the PO as below,

$$ \min_{\beta\in\mathbbm{R}^{p},u\in\mathbbm{R}^{n}}\max_{v\in\mathbbm{R}^{n}}\frac{1}{n}1^{\intercal}\rho(u)-\frac{1}{n}y^{\intercal}u+\frac{1}{n}v^{\intercal}u-\frac{1}{n}v^{\intercal}XP\beta-\frac{1}{n}v^{\intercal}XP^{\perp}\beta. $$

Before we apply CGMT, we remark that we can simply assume the feasible sets of $v,u$ and $\beta$ are convex and compact, following Lemma A.1 and Lemma A.2 in Thrampoulidis et al., (2018). For simplicity, we omit the details here and write the AO as:

$$ (\text{AO})\ \ \ \min_{\beta\in\mathbbm{R}^{p},u\in\mathbbm{R}^{n}}\max_{v\in\mathbbm{R}^{n}}\frac{1}{n}1^{\intercal}\rho(u)-\frac{1}{n}y^{\intercal}u+\frac{1}{n}v^{\intercal}(u-XP\beta)-\frac{1}{n}(v^{\intercal}h||P^{\perp}\beta||+||v||g^{\intercal}P^{\perp}\beta), $$

in which $h$ and $g$ are independent, following $N(0,I_{n})$ and $N(0,I_{p})$ , respectively.

We proceed to simplify the AO. Let $r=||v||/\sqrt{n}$ . Maximizing with respect to the direction of $v$ , the AO can be written as

$$ \min_{\beta\in\mathbbm{R}^{p},u\in\mathbbm{R}^{n}}\max_{r\geq 0}\frac{1}{n}1^{\intercal}\rho(u)-\frac{1}{n}y^{\intercal}u-\frac{r}{\sqrt{n}}g^{\intercal}P^{\perp}\beta+r\left|\left|\frac{u}{\sqrt{n}}-\frac{XP\beta}{\sqrt{n}}-\frac{||P^{\perp}\beta||h}{\sqrt{n}}\right|\right|. $$

By Lemma A.3 in Thrampoulidis et al., (2018), we swap the order of min-max in the optimization problem (52). Let $\sigma=||P^{\perp}\beta||/\sqrt{\kappa}$ , $\alpha=\left<\beta,\beta^{\star}\right>/||\beta^{\star}||^{2}$ , then $P\beta=\alpha\beta^{\star}$ . Optimizing with respect to the direction of $P^{\perp}\beta$ , we can further simplify the optimization problem (52) as

$$ \max_{r\geq 0}\min_{u\in\mathbbm{R}^{n},\sigma\geq 0,\alpha\in\mathbbm{R}}\frac{1}{n}1^{\intercal}\rho(u)-\frac{1}{n}y^{\intercal}u+\frac{r\sqrt{p}}{n}||g||\sigma+r\left|\left|\frac{u}{\sqrt{n}}-\frac{\alpha X\beta^{\star}}{\sqrt{n}}-\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}\sigma h}{\sqrt{n}}\right|\right|. $$

Using the square-root trick, i.e., $\sqrt{x}=\inf_{\delta>0}\left\{\frac{\delta}{2}+\frac{x}{2\delta}\right\}$ , we obtain

$$ \max_{r\geq 0}\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}u\in\mathbbm{R}^{n},\sigma\geq 0\\
\alpha\in\mathbbm{R},\ \delta>0\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{n}1^{\intercal}\rho(u)-\frac{1}{n}y^{\intercal}u+\frac{r\sqrt{p}}{n}||g||\sigma+\frac{\delta r}{2}\left|\left|\frac{u}{\sqrt{n}}-\frac{\alpha X\beta^{\star}}{\sqrt{n}}-\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}\sigma h}{\sqrt{n}}\right|\right|^{2}+\frac{r}{2\delta}. $$

We proceed to optimize with respect to $u$ . Based on completion of square, we have

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{1}{n}y^{\intercal}u+\frac{\delta r}{2} \displaystyle\left|\left|\frac{u}{\sqrt{n}}-\frac{\alpha X\beta^{\star}}{\sqrt{n}}-\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}\sigma h}{\sqrt{n}}\right|\right|^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{\delta r}{2n}\left|\left|u-\alpha X\beta^{\star}-\sqrt{\kappa}\sigma h-\frac{y}{\delta r}\right|\right|^{2}-\frac{||y||^{2}}{2n\delta r}-\frac{\alpha}{n}y^{\intercal}X\beta^{\star}-\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}}{n}\sigma y^{\intercal}h. $$

Optimizing with respect to the direction of $u$ , the AO can be simplified as below,

$$ \displaystyle\max_{r\geq 0}\min_{\sigma\geq 0,\alpha\in\mathbbm{R},\delta>0}\mathcal{R}_{n}(\sigma,\alpha,\delta,r) \displaystyle:=\frac{r\sqrt{p}}{n}||g||\sigma+\frac{r}{2\delta}-\frac{||y||^{2}}{2n\delta r}-\frac{\alpha}{n}y^{\intercal}X\beta^{\star}-\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}}{n}\sigma y^{\intercal}h \displaystyle+\frac{1}{n}M_{\rho}\Big(\alpha X\beta^{\star}+\sigma\sqrt{\kappa}h+\frac{y}{\delta r},\frac{1}{\delta r}\Big), $$

in which the function $M_{\rho}$ is applied in an element-wise fashion. We now reduce the original vector optimization problem into a scalar optimization problem. Since the objective function is convex in $\sigma,\alpha,\delta$ and concave in $r$ , we can swap the order of min and max.

We proceed to further simplify the AO by invoking asymptotics. By the law of large numbers, we have the following simple results,

$$ \displaystyle\text{(a)} \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}||y||^{2}\overset{p}{\to}\mathbbm{E}(y^{2}); \displaystyle\text{(b)} \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}y^{\intercal}X\beta^{\star}\overset{p}{\to}\mathbbm{E}(y_{i}X_{i}^{\intercal}\beta^{\star}); \displaystyle\text{(c)} \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}M_{\rho}\Big(\alpha X\beta^{\star}+\sigma\sqrt{\kappa}h+\frac{y}{\delta r},\frac{1}{\delta r}\Big)\overset{p}{\to}\mathbbm{E}\Big[M_{\rho}\Big(\alpha\gamma Z_{1}+\sigma\sqrt{\kappa}Z_{2}+\frac{y}{\delta r},\frac{1}{\delta r}\Big)\Big], \displaystyle\text{(d)} \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}y^{\intercal}h=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}y^{\intercal}h=O_{p}({1}/{\sqrt{n}}), \displaystyle\text{(e)} \displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{p}}{n}||g||=\frac{p}{n}\frac{||g||}{\sqrt{p}}\overset{p}{\to}\frac{p}{n}=\kappa. $$

Based upon these facts, $\mathcal{R}_{n}$ converges in probability to

$$ D(\sigma,\alpha,\delta,r):=r\kappa\sigma+\frac{r}{2\delta}-\frac{1}{2\delta r}\mathbbm{E}(y^{2})-\alpha\mathbbm{E}(yX^{\intercal}\beta^{\star})+\mathbbm{E}\Big[M_{\rho}\Big(\alpha\gamma Z_{1}+\sigma\sqrt{\kappa}Z_{2}+\frac{y}{\delta r},\frac{1}{\delta r}\Big)\Big]. $$

We note that the objective function $D(\sigma,\alpha,\delta,r)$ is convex in $\sigma,\alpha,\delta$ and concave in $r$ , since the convexity is preserved through point-wise limit. The covergence of the optimizers can be established based on the same arguments as in Lemma B.1 and Lemma A.5 in Thrampoulidis et al., (2018). This completes the proof of Lemma A.1.

#### A.2.2 Proof of Proposition 3.1

The proof of Proposition 3.1 is essentially the same as the proof of Theorem 3.1 in Zhao et al., (2020). Denote $\Sigma=LL^{\intercal}$ as the Cholesky decomposition of the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ . Let

$$ \theta^{\star}=L^{\intercal}\beta^{\star},\ \ \ \widehat{\theta}=L^{\intercal}\widehat{\beta}, $$

in which $\widehat{\beta}$ is the MLE of the true regression coefficient $\beta^{\star}$ . By Proposition 2.1 in Zhao et al., (2020), $\widehat{\theta}$ has the same distribution as the MLE of the underlying GLM with true regression coefficient $\theta^{\star}$ and features drawn i.i.d from $N(0,I_{p})$ . We note that it is sufficient to consider the case $\Sigma=I_{p}$ , as the general result follows from the following relationship,

$$ \tau_{j}\frac{\widehat{\beta}_{j}-\alpha_{\star}\beta_{j}^{\star}}{\sigma_{\star}}=\frac{\widehat{\theta}_{j}-\alpha_{\star}\theta_{j}^{\star}}{\sigma_{\star}}. $$

For $j\in[p]$ , we have the following decomposition,

$$ \frac{\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}_{j}-\alpha_{\star}\theta_{j}^{\star})}{\sigma_{\star}}=\frac{\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}_{j}-\alpha_{n}\theta_{j}^{\star})}{\sigma_{n}}\frac{\sigma_{n}}{\sigma_{\star}}+\frac{\sqrt{n}(\alpha_{n}-\alpha_{\star})\theta_{j}^{\star}}{\sigma_{\star}}. $$

Using the same arguments as in the proof of Theorem 3.1 in Zhao et al., (2020), we can show that the first term asymptotically behaves as the standard normal distribution, whereas the second term asymptotically vanishes. This completes the proof of Proposition 3.1.

### A.3 Proof of Proposition 3.2

In addition to the notations introduced in Equation (59), we require the following notations for the ease of presentation. Let $\langle u,v\rangle_{\Sigma}=u^{\intercal}\Sigma v$ for any $u,v\in\mathbbm{R}^{p}$ , and $||u||^{2}_{\Sigma}=u^{\intercal}\Sigma u$ . We introduce the following random vector,

$$ \displaystyle\xi=W-\frac{1}{\gamma_{n}^{2}}\langle W,\beta^{\star}\rangle_{\Sigma}\beta^{\star}, $$

in which $W$ follows $N(0,\Theta)$ , independent to everything else. Recall that $\gamma_{n}^{2}=\text{Var}(x_{i}^{\intercal}\beta^{\star})$ calibrates the signal strength, and we assume $\gamma_{n}\to\gamma$ as $n,p\to\infty$ . We define

$$ \widetilde{V}_{j}=\frac{\sqrt{p}V_{j}}{||\xi||_{\Sigma}}\ \ \ \text{with}\ \ \ V_{j}=\tau_{j}W_{j}, $$

for $j\in[p]$ where $\tau_{j}^{2}=1/\Theta_{jj}$ . The random vector $V$ follows $N(0,R)$ with $R_{ij}=\tau_{i}\tau_{j}\Theta_{ij}$ . With a bit abuse of notation, we denote $\kappa=2p/n\in(0,1)$ as the ratio of the dimension over the sample size after data splitting.

We define the normalized MLE $T_{j}$ as well as its approximation $\widetilde{T}_{j}$ as below,

$$ T_{j}=\frac{\sqrt{n}\widehat{\tau}_{j}\widehat{\beta}_{j}}{\sigma_{\star}},\ \ \ \widetilde{T}_{j}=\frac{\sqrt{n\kappa}\tau_{j}\widehat{\beta}_{j}}{\sigma_{n}} $$

for $j\in[p]$ , in which $\sigma_{\star}$ is the unique optimizer of the optimization problem defined in (46). Without changing the selection result obtained via Algorithm 1, we multiply the normalized MLE defined in Equation (14) by a constant factor so that it follows the standard normal distribution asymptotically. Let $\widetilde{M}_{j}$ be the corresponding approximated mirror statistic constructed based upon $\widetilde{T}^{(1)}_{j}$ and $\widetilde{T}^{(2)}_{j}$ .

#### A.3.1 Technical lemmas

#### Lemma A.2.

$\widetilde{T}_{S_{0}}\overset{d}{=}\widetilde{V}_{S_{0}}$ .

Proof of Lemma A.2. We note that a simple calculation yields

$$ L^{-\intercal}P_{\theta^{\star}}^{\perp}Z\overset{d}{=}\xi,\ \ \ ||P_{\theta^{\star}}^{\perp}Z||_{2}=||\xi||_{\Sigma}, $$

in which $Z$ following $N(0,I_{p})$ is independent to everything else. Let $\Lambda_{S_{0}}$ be a $p_{0}\times p_{0}$ diagonal matrix, of which the diagonal elements are $\tau_{j}$ for $j\in S_{0}$ . By the stochastic representation (Lemma 2.1, Proposition A.1) in Zhao et al., (2020), we have

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{T}_{S_{0}} \displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{p}\Lambda_{S_{0}}\widehat{\beta}_{S_{0}}}{\sigma_{n}}=\frac{\sqrt{p}\Lambda_{S_{0}}(L^{-\intercal}\widehat{\theta})_{S_{0}}}{\sigma_{n}} \displaystyle\overset{d}{=}\frac{\sqrt{p}\Lambda_{S_{0}}(L^{-\intercal}P_{\theta^{\star}}^{\perp}Z)_{S_{0}}}{||P_{\theta^{\star}}^{\perp}Z||_{2}}\overset{d}{=}\frac{\sqrt{p}\Lambda_{S_{0}}\xi_{S_{0}}}{||\xi||_{\Sigma}}\overset{d}{=}\widetilde{V}_{S_{0}}. $$

This completes the proof of Lemma A.2.

#### Lemma A.3.

Under Assumption 3.1, there exists a constant $c>0$ such that for $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ , we have

$$ \mathbbm{P}\left(\max_{j\in[p]}\left|{\widehat{\tau}_{j}^{2}}/{\tau_{j}^{2}}-1\right|>\epsilon\right)\leq p\exp(-c(n/2-p+1)\epsilon^{2}). $$

Proof of Lemma A.3. By Assumption 3.1, we have

$$ \displaystyle\min_{j\in[p]}{\tau_{j}^{2}}=1/\max_{j\in[p]}\Theta_{jj}\geq 1/\sigma_{\max}(\Theta)=\sigma_{\min}(\Sigma)\geq 1/C>0, \displaystyle\max_{j\in[p]}{\tau_{j}^{2}}=1/\min_{j\in[p]}\Theta_{jj}\leq 1/\sigma_{\min}(\Theta)=\sigma_{\max}(\Sigma)\leq C<\infty. $$

Thus, it is sufficient for us to consider $\max_{j\in[p]}\left|\widehat{\tau}_{j}^{2}-\tau_{j}^{2}\right|$ . Since $\text{RSS}_{j}\sim\tau_{j}^{2}\chi^{2}_{n/2-p+1}$ , by the union bound and a Bernstein-type inequality, for any $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbbm{P}\left(\max_{j\in[p]}\left|{\widehat{\tau}_{j}^{2}}-\tau_{j}^{2}\right|>\epsilon\right) \displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=1}^{p}\mathbbm{P}\left(\left|{\widehat{\tau}_{j}^{2}}-\tau_{j}^{2}\right|>\epsilon\right) \displaystyle\leq p\exp(-c(n/2-p+1)\epsilon^{2}) $$

for some constant $c>0$ .

#### Lemma A.4.

Under Assumption 3.1, as $n,p\to\infty$ , we have

$$ \sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R},j\in S_{0}}|\mathbbm{P}(T_{j}>t)-Q(t)|\longrightarrow 0 $$

Proof of Lemma A.4. Without loss of generality, we assume $t>0$ . For $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ , we condition on the event $E_{1}\cap E_{2}$ , in which

$$ \displaystyle E_{1}=\{|\sigma_{n}/\sqrt{\kappa}-\sigma_{\star}|<\epsilon\}, \displaystyle E_{2}=\big\{\max_{j\in[p]}\left|{\widehat{\tau}_{j}}/{\tau_{j}}-1\right|<\epsilon\big\}. $$

For large enough $n$ and $p$ , $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ hold with high probability according to Lemma A.1 and Lemma A.3, respectively. Conditioning on the events $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\max_{j\in[p]}|T_{j}/\widetilde{T}_{j}-1| \displaystyle\leq\max_{j\in[p]}|\widehat{\tau}_{j}/\tau_{j}||\sigma_{n}/\sqrt{\kappa}-\sigma_{\star}|/\sigma_{\star}+\max_{j\in[p]}\left|{\widehat{\tau}_{j}}/{\tau_{j}}-1\right| \displaystyle\leq(\epsilon+1)\epsilon/\sigma_{\star}+\epsilon. $$

Consequently, we have

$$ \max_{j\in[p]}|T_{j}/\widetilde{T}_{j}-1|\overset{p}{\to}0. $$

We proceed to show that

$$ \max_{j\in[p]}\left|\widetilde{V}_{j}/V_{j}-1\right|=\left|\frac{\sqrt{p}}{||\xi||_{\Sigma}}-1\right|\overset{p}{\to}0, $$

in which by definition, $V_{j}$ follows the standard normal distribution. Indeed, by the definition of $\xi$ in Equation (62), we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{||\xi||^{2}_{\Sigma}}{p} \displaystyle=\frac{||W||^{2}_{\Sigma}}{p}-\frac{1}{p}\langle W,\frac{\beta^{\star}}{\gamma_{n}}\rangle_{\Sigma}^{2}. $$

The second term converges to 0 in probability, since $\langle W,{\beta^{\star}}/{\gamma_{n}}\rangle_{\Sigma}$ follows the standard normal distribution. For the first term, we have

$$ \frac{||W||^{2}_{\Sigma}}{p}=\frac{1}{p}{W}^{\intercal}\Sigma W=\frac{Z^{\intercal}Z}{p}\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}1. $$

It follows that

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{t>0,\ j\in S_{0}}\left|\mathbbm{P}(T_{j}>t)-Q(t)\right| \displaystyle\leq\sup_{t>0,\ j\in S_{0}}\left|\mathbbm{P}(T_{j}>t)-\mathbbm{P}(\widetilde{T}_{j}>t)\right| \displaystyle+\sup_{t>0,\ j\in S_{0}}\left|\mathbbm{P}(\widetilde{T}_{j}>t)-Q(t)\right| \displaystyle=\sup_{t>0,\ j\in S_{0}}\left|\mathbbm{P}(T_{j}>t)-\mathbbm{P}(\widetilde{T}_{j}>t)\right| \displaystyle+\sup_{t>0,\ j\in S_{0}}\left|\mathbbm{P}(\widetilde{V}_{j}>t)-\mathbbm{P}(V_{j}>t)\right| \displaystyle\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}0. $$

The equality follows from Lemma A.2. The convergence in the last line follows from Equations (73) and (74) (detailed arguments can be found in Equations (82) and (83)). This completes the proof of Lemma A.4.

#### Lemma A.5.

If Equation (70) holds, as $n,p\to\infty$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R},\ j\in S_{0}}\left|\mathbbm{P}(M_{j}>t)-H(t)\right|\longrightarrow 0. $$

Proof of Lemma A.5. Without loss of generality, we assume $t>0$ . Let $Z^{(1)}$ and $Z^{(2)}$ be two independent random variables following the standard normal distribution, which are also independent to $T_{j}^{(1)}$ and $T_{j}^{(2)}$ . For any $\epsilon>0$ , for large enough $n$ and $p$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbbm{P}(M_{j}>t) \displaystyle=\mathbbm{P}\Big(T_{j}^{(2)}>I_{t}\big(T_{j}^{(1)}\big),\ T_{j}^{(1)}>0\Big)+\mathbbm{P}\Big(T_{j}^{(2)}<-I_{t}\big(T_{j}^{(1)}\big),\ T_{j}^{(1)}<0\Big) \displaystyle\leq\mathbbm{P}\Big(Z^{(2)}>I_{t}\big(T_{j}^{(1)}\big),\ T_{j}^{(1)}>0\Big)+\mathbbm{P}\Big(Z^{(2)}<-I_{t}\big(T_{j}^{(1)}\big),\ T_{j}^{(1)}<0\Big)+\epsilon \displaystyle=\mathbbm{P}\Big(\text{sign}\big(T_{j}^{(1)}Z^{(2)}\big)f\big(T_{j}^{(1)},Z^{(2)}\big)>t\Big)+\epsilon \displaystyle=\mathbbm{P}\Big(T_{j}^{(1)}>I_{t}\big(Z^{(2)}\big),\ Z^{(2)}>0\Big)+\mathbbm{P}\Big(T_{j}^{(1)}<-I_{t}\big(Z^{(2)}\big),\ Z^{(2)}<0\Big)+\epsilon \displaystyle\leq\mathbbm{P}\Big(Z^{(1)}>I_{t}\big(Z^{(2)}\big),\ Z^{(2)}>0\Big)+\mathbbm{P}\Big(Z^{(1)}<-I_{t}\big(Z^{(2)}\big),\ Z^{(2)}<0\Big)+2\epsilon \displaystyle=H(t)+2\epsilon, $$

where all the equalities follow from the fact that $f(u,v)$ is monotonically increasing with respect to $|u|$ and $|v|$ , and the two inequalities follow from Equation (70) as well as the independence between the random variables. Similarly, we can show that $\mathbbm{P}(M_{j}>t)\geq H(t)-2\epsilon$ for large enough $n$ and $p$ . This completes the proof of Lemma A.5.

#### Lemma A.6.

Under Assumption 3.1, as $n,p\to\infty$ , we have

$$ \sup_{i,j\in S_{0},\ t_{1},t_{2}\in\mathbbm{R}}\left|\mathbbm{P}(T_{i}>t_{1},T_{j}>t_{2})-\mathbbm{P}(V_{i}>t_{1},V_{j}>t_{2})\right|\longrightarrow 0. $$

Proof of Lemma A.6. Without loss of generality, we assume $t_{1}>0$ and $t_{2}>0$ . For any given $\epsilon>0$ , denote

$$ \displaystyle E_{1}=\Big\{\max_{k\in[p]}|T_{k}/\widetilde{T}_{k}-1|\leq\epsilon\Big\},\ \ \ E_{2}=\Big\{\max_{k\in[p]}|\widetilde{V}_{k}/V_{k}-1|\leq\epsilon\Big\}. $$

By Equations (73) and (74), for large enough $n$ and $p$ , we have $\mathbbm{P}(E_{1})\geq 1-\epsilon$ and $\mathbbm{P}(E_{2})\geq 1-\epsilon$ . For $i,j\in S_{0}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbbm{P}(T_{i}>t_{1},T_{j}>t_{2}) \displaystyle\geq\mathbbm{P}(T_{i}>t_{1},T_{j}>t_{2}\mid E_{1})\mathbbm{P}(E_{1}) \displaystyle\geq\mathbbm{P}\Big(\widetilde{T}_{i}>\frac{t_{1}}{1-\epsilon},\widetilde{T}_{j}>\frac{t_{2}}{1-\epsilon}\ \big|\ E_{1}\Big)\mathbbm{P}(E_{1}) \displaystyle\geq\mathbbm{P}\Big(\widetilde{T}_{i}>\frac{t_{1}}{1-\epsilon},\widetilde{T}_{j}>\frac{t_{2}}{1-\epsilon}\Big)-\epsilon \displaystyle=\mathbbm{P}\Big(\widetilde{V}_{i}>\frac{t_{1}}{1-\epsilon},\widetilde{V}_{j}>\frac{t_{2}}{1-\epsilon}\Big)-\epsilon \displaystyle\geq\mathbbm{P}\Big(\widetilde{V}_{i}>\frac{t_{1}}{1-\epsilon},\widetilde{V}_{j}>\frac{t_{2}}{1-\epsilon}\ \big|\ E_{2}\Big)\mathbbm{P}(E_{2})-\epsilon \displaystyle\geq\mathbbm{P}\Big(V_{i}>\frac{t_{1}}{(1-\epsilon)^{2}},V_{j}>\frac{t_{2}}{(1-\epsilon)^{2}}\ \big|\ E_{2}\Big)\mathbbm{P}(E_{2})-\epsilon \displaystyle\geq\mathbbm{P}\Big(V_{i}>\frac{t_{1}}{(1-\epsilon)^{2}},V_{j}>\frac{t_{2}}{(1-\epsilon)^{2}}\Big)-2\epsilon, $$

in which the equality in the fourth line follows from Lemma A.2. Similarly, we have

Combining Equations (82) and (83) leads to the claim in Lemma A.6.

#### Lemma A.7.

Under Assumption 3.1, as $n,p\to\infty$ , we have

$$ \sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}\textnormal{Var}\bigg(\frac{1}{p_{0}}\sum_{j\in S_{0}}\mathbbm{1}(M_{j}>t)\bigg)\leq\frac{1}{4p_{0}}+O(||R_{S_{0}}||_{1})+o(1), $$

in which $||R_{S_{0}}||_{1}=\sum_{i,j\in S_{0}}R_{ij}/p_{0}^{2}$ .

Proof of Lemma A.7. Without loss of generality, we assume $t>0$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}\textnormal{Var}\bigg(\frac{1}{p_{0}}\sum_{j\in S_{0}}\mathbbm{1}(M_{j}>t)\bigg) \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{p_{0}^{2}}\sum_{j\in S_{0}}\sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}\text{Var}(\mathbbm{1}(M_{j}>t)) \displaystyle+\frac{1}{p_{0}^{2}}\sum_{i\neq j\in S_{0}}\sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}\text{Cov}(\mathbbm{1}(M_{i}>t),\mathbbm{1}(M_{j}>t)). $$

Using the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality, the first term is upper bounded by $1/(4p_{0})$ . For the second term, since

$$ \displaystyle\text{Cov}(\mathbbm{1}(M_{i}>t),\mathbbm{1}(M_{j}>t)) \displaystyle\leq\left|\mathbbm{P}(M_{i}>t,M_{j}>t)-H^{2}(t)\right| \displaystyle+\left|\mathbbm{P}(M_{i}>t)\mathbbm{P}(M_{j}>t)-H^{2}(t)\right|, $$

by Lemma A.5, it is sufficient for us to show that for $i,j\in S_{0}$ and $i\neq j$ ,

$$ \sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}\left|\mathbbm{P}(M_{i}>t,M_{j}>t)-H^{2}(t)\right|\leq O(|R_{ij}|)+o(1). $$

By Condition 2.2, we have the following decomposition based on the signs of $T^{(1)}_{i}$ and $T^{(1)}_{j}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbbm{P}(M_{i}>t,M_{j}>t) \displaystyle=\mathbbm{P}\left(T_{i}^{(2)}>I_{t}\big(T_{i}^{(1)}\big),\ \ T_{j}^{(2)}>I_{t}\big(T_{j}^{(1)}\big),\ \ T_{i}^{(1)}>0,T_{j}^{(1)}>0\right) \displaystyle+\hskip 1.42271pt\mathbbm{P}\left(T_{i}^{(2)}>I_{t}\big(T_{i}^{(1)}\big),\ \ T_{j}^{(2)}<-I_{t}\big(T_{j}^{(1)}\big),T_{i}^{(1)}>0,T_{j}^{(1)}<0\right) \displaystyle+\hskip 1.42271pt\mathbbm{P}\left(T_{i}^{(2)}<-I_{t}\big(T_{i}^{(1)}\big),T_{j}^{(2)}>I_{t}\big(T_{j}^{(1)}\big),\ \ T_{i}^{(1)}<0,T_{j}^{(1)}>0\right) \displaystyle+\hskip 1.42271pt\mathbbm{P}\left(T_{i}^{(2)}<-I_{t}\big(T_{i}^{(1)}\big),T_{j}^{(2)}<-I_{t}\big(T_{j}^{(1)}\big),T_{i}^{(1)}<0,T_{j}^{(1)}<0\right) \displaystyle:=I_{1}+I_{2}+I_{3}+I_{4}. $$

Denote $\Phi_{r}$ and $\phi_{r}$ as the CDF and pdf of the bivariate normal distribution with variances 1 and correlation $r$ , respectively. Let $\phi^{(n)}$ be the $n$ -th derivative of $\phi$ . Recall the Mehler’s identity (Kotz et al.,, 2000), that is, for any $t_{1},t_{2}\in\mathbbm{R}$ ,

$$ \Phi_{r}(t_{1},t_{2})=\Phi(t_{1})\Phi(t_{2})+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{r^{n}}{n!}\phi^{(n-1)}(t_{1})\phi^{(n-1)}(t_{2}). $$

For $I_{1}$ , we have the following upper bound,

$$ \displaystyle I_{1} \displaystyle=\mathbbm{E}\left[\mathbbm{P}\big(T_{i}^{(2)}>I_{t}(x),\ T_{j}^{(2)}>I_{t}(y)\big)\ \big|\ T_{i}^{(1)}=x>0,\ T_{j}^{(1)}=y>0\right] \displaystyle=\mathbbm{E}\left[\mathbbm{P}\big(V_{i}^{(2)}>I_{t}(x),\ V_{j}^{(2)}>I_{t}(y)\big)\ \big|\ T_{i}^{(1)}=x>0,\ T_{j}^{(1)}=y>0\right]+o(1) \displaystyle\leq\mathbbm{E}\left[Q(I_{t}(x))Q(I_{t}(y))\ \big|\ T_{i}^{(1)}=x>0,\ T_{j}^{(1)}=y>0\right]+O(|R_{ij}|)+o(1). $$

The second line follows from Lemma A.6. The third line follows from the Mehler’s identity and Lemma 1 in Azriel and Schwartzman, (2015), i.e.,

$$ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\left[\sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}\phi^{(n-1)}(t)\right]^{2}}{n!}<\infty. $$

Similarly, we can upper bound $I_{2}$ , $I_{3}$ and $I_{4}$ . Combining the four upper bounds together, we obtain an upper bound on $\mathbbm{P}(M_{i}>t,M_{j}>t)$ specified as below,

#### Lemma A.9.

For the response vector $y$ , we consider fitting two GLMs with respect to the set of features $X=(Z,X_{1},\ldots,X_{p})\in\mathbbm{R}^{n\times(p+1)}$ (full model), and $\widetilde{X}=(X_{1},\ldots,X_{p})\in\mathbbm{R}^{n\times p}$ (reduced model), respectively, in which each row of $\widetilde{X}$ are i.i.d. samples from $N(0,I_{p})$ , and $Z$ is a null feature following $N(0,I_{n})$ . Denote the MLEs for the full model and the reduced model as $\widehat{\beta}\in\mathbbm{R}^{p+1}$ and $\widetilde{\beta}\in\mathbbm{R}^{p}$ , respectively. Denote the difference between the two MLEs as $\Delta=\widehat{\beta}_{2:(p+1)}-\widetilde{\beta}$ , then we have

$$ ||\Delta||_{\infty}=O_{p}\big(n^{-1+o(1)}\big). $$

Proof of Lemma A.9. The proof relies heavily on the theoretical results derived in Sur et al., (2019) (see Section 7 therein), and the main technical tool is the leave-one-out analysis. In the following, we sketch the proof of Lemma A.9, and refer the readers to the results in Sur et al., (2019) for complete details.

We first construct a surrogate of $\widehat{\beta}$ as below following Equation (86) in Sur et al., (2019),

$$ \widetilde{b}=\left[\begin{matrix}0\\
\widetilde{\beta}\end{matrix}\right]+\widetilde{b}_{1}\left[\begin{matrix}1\\
-\widetilde{G}^{-1}w\end{matrix}\right], $$

in which

$$ \widetilde{G}=\frac{1}{n}\widetilde{X}^{\intercal}D_{\widetilde{\beta}}\widetilde{X},\ \ \ \ \ \ w=\frac{1}{n}\widetilde{X}^{\intercal}D_{\widetilde{\beta}}Z, $$

where $D_{\widetilde{\beta}}$ is a $n\times n$ diagonal matrix with entries $\rho^{\prime\prime}(\widetilde{x}_{i}^{\intercal}\widetilde{\beta})$ for $i\in[n]$ , and $\widetilde{b}_{1}$ is defined as below following Equation (91) in Sur et al., (2019),

$$ \widetilde{b}_{1}=\frac{Z^{\intercal}\widetilde{r}}{Z^{\intercal}D_{\widetilde{\beta}}^{1/2}HD_{\widetilde{\beta}}^{1/2}Z}, $$

where

$$ H=I-\frac{1}{n}D_{\widetilde{\beta}}^{1/2}\widetilde{X}\widetilde{G}^{-1}\widetilde{X}^{\intercal}D_{\widetilde{\beta}}^{1/2}\ \ \ \text{and}\ \ \ \widetilde{r}_{i}=y_{i}-\rho^{\prime}(\widetilde{x}_{i}^{\intercal}\widetilde{\beta}),\ \ \ i\in[n]. $$

By Theorem 8 and similar arguments in Section 7.4 in Sur et al., (2019), we have

$$ \displaystyle||\Delta||_{\infty} \displaystyle\leq||\widehat{\beta}-\widetilde{b}||_{\infty}+||\widetilde{b}_{1}\widetilde{G}^{-1}w||_{\infty} \displaystyle\lesssim n^{-1+o(1)}+n^{-1/2+o(1)}||\widetilde{G}^{-1}w||_{\infty}. $$

Thus it remains to bound $||\widetilde{G}^{-1}w||_{\infty}$ .

We note that both $\widetilde{X}$ and $D_{\widetilde{\beta}}$ are independent to $Z$ . Therefore, conditioning on $\widetilde{X}$ , $\widetilde{G}^{-1}w$ follows a multivariate normal distribution with mean 0, and covariance matrix $\Sigma_{Z}$ specified as below,

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma_{Z}=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\widetilde{G}^{-1}\widetilde{X}^{\intercal}D_{\widetilde{\beta}}^{2}\widetilde{X}\widetilde{G}^{-1} \displaystyle\prec\sup_{i\in[n]}|\rho^{\prime\prime}(\widetilde{x}_{i}^{\intercal}\widetilde{\beta})|\frac{1}{n^{2}}\widetilde{G}^{-1}\widetilde{X}^{\intercal}D_{\widetilde{\beta}}\widetilde{X}\widetilde{G}^{-1} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sup_{i\in[n]}|\rho^{\prime\prime}(\widetilde{x}_{i}^{\intercal}\widetilde{\beta})|\widetilde{G}^{-1}. $$

By Lemma 7 in Sur et al., (2019), we have $\sigma_{\min}(\widetilde{G})>\lambda$ with high probability, in which $\lambda$ is some positive constant. This implies $\sigma_{\max}(\Sigma_{Z})=O_{p}(1/n)$ , which further leads to $||\widetilde{G}^{-1}w||_{\infty}\lesssim\sqrt{{\log n}/{n}}$ . Thus we complete the proof of Lemma A.9 via

$$ ||\Delta||_{\infty}\lesssim n^{-1+o(1)}+n^{-1/2+o(1)}\sqrt{{\log n}/{n}}=O_{p}(n^{-1+o(1)}). $$

#### Lemma A.14.

For any $\epsilon>0$ , by Proposition 5.1 in Javanmard and Montanari, (2013) (also see Van de Geer et al., (2014)), there exists an $n_{\epsilon}\in\mathbbm{N}_{+}$ such that for $n\geq n_{\epsilon}$ , we have

$$ \mathbbm{P}\left(||\widehat{\Theta}-\Theta||_{\infty}\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{\log p}}\right)\geq 1-\epsilon. $$

In the following, we condition on this high probability event. Denote $v=\Theta^{\top}e_{i},u=\Theta^{\top}e_{j},\delta=(\Theta-\hat{\Theta})^{\top}e_{i},\eta=(\Theta-\hat{\Theta})^{\top}e_{j}$ . We have the following decomposition,

$$ \displaystyle\Lambda_{ij}-\Theta_{ij} \displaystyle=(v-\delta)^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}(u-\eta)-\Theta_{ij} \displaystyle=\big(v^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}u-\Theta_{ij}\big)-v^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}\eta-\delta^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}u+\delta^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}\eta. $$

We proceed to bound each term. For the term $v^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}u-\Theta_{ij}$ , since $\mathbbm{E}[v^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}u]=v^{\top}\Sigma u=\Theta_{ij}$ , it follows that

$$ \displaystyle v^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}u-\Theta_{ij} \displaystyle=v^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}u-\mathbbm{E}[v^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}u] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}e_{i}^{\top}\Theta\left(x_{k}x_{k}^{\top}-\mathbbm{E}[x_{k}x^{\top}_{k}]\right)\Theta^{\top}e_{j} $$

$$ \displaystyle||\xi_{k}||_{\psi_{1}}\leq 2||(e_{i}^{\top}\Theta x_{k})^{2}||_{\psi_{1}}\leq 4||e_{i}^{\top}\Theta x_{k}||_{\psi_{2}}^{2}\leq K $$

for some constant $K>0$ , where the first inequality follows from Vershynin, (2010) (Remark 5.18), the second inequality follows from Lemma C.1 in Javanmard and Montanari, (2013), and the last inequality follows from Assumption 4.1 (2). $$ \mathbbm{P}\left(\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\xi_{k}\right|\geq t\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-cn\min\left(\frac{t^{2}}{K^{2}},\frac{t}{K}\right)\right). $$

Plugging in $t=1/{\sqrt{\log p}}$ and employing the union bound, we obtain

$$ \mathbbm{P}\left(\max_{i,j\in[p]}\left|v^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}u-\Theta_{ij}\right|\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{\log p}}\right)\leq 2p^{2}\exp\left(-c_{2}\frac{n}{\log p}\right) $$

for some constant $c_{2}>0$ .

Next we consider the term $\delta^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}\eta$ . Since $\hat{\Sigma}\succeq 0$ , it is sufficient for us to bound both $\delta^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}\delta$ and $\eta^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}\eta$ by the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality. Notice that

$$ \delta^{\top}\Sigma\delta=\sum_{i,j\in[p]}\hat{\Sigma}_{ij}\delta_{i}\delta_{j}\leq|\hat{\Sigma}|_{\infty}||\delta||_{1}^{2}\leq|\hat{\Sigma}|_{\infty}||\Theta-\hat{\Theta}||_{\infty}^{2}\leq\frac{|\hat{\Sigma}|_{\infty}}{\log p}. $$

We proceed to bound the tail probability $\mathbbm{P}(|\hat{\Sigma}|_{\infty}\geq 2)$ . First, using the union bound, we have

$$ \mathbbm{P}(|\hat{\Sigma}|_{\infty}\geq 2)\leq\sum_{i,j\in[p]}\mathbbm{P}(|\hat{\Sigma}_{ij}|\geq 2)\leq\sum_{i,j\in[p]}\mathbbm{P}(|\hat{\Sigma}_{ij}-\mathbbm{E}\hat{\Sigma}_{ij}|\geq 1). $$

Denote $\xi_{k}=e_{i}^{\top}x_{k}x_{k}^{\top}e_{j}-\Sigma_{ij}$ for $k\in[n]$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle||\xi_{k}||_{\psi_{1}} \displaystyle\leq 2||(e_{i}^{\top}x_{k})^{2}||_{\psi_{1}}\leq 4||e_{i}^{\top}x_{k}||^{2}_{\psi_{2}}\leq 4||e_{i}^{\top}\Theta^{-1/2}\Theta^{1/2}x_{k}||^{2}_{\psi_{2}}\leq K $$

for some constant $K>0$ . Thus $\xi_{k}$ ‘s are independent sub-exponential random variables. By the Bernstein inequality, we have

$$ \mathbbm{P}(|\hat{\Sigma}|_{\infty}\geq 2)\leq 2p^{2}\exp(-c_{4}n) $$

for some constant $c_{4}>0$ . We remark that although $\delta=(\Theta-\hat{\Theta})^{\top}e_{i}$ is implicitly associated with the index $i$ , the upper bound $|\hat{\Sigma}|_{\infty}||\Theta-\hat{\Theta}||_{\infty}^{2}$ in Equation (133) is irrelevant to the index $i$ . Therefore, we have shown that

$$ \mathbbm{P}\left(\max_{i,j\in[p]}{|\delta^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}\eta|}\geq{\frac{2}{\log p}}\right)\leq 4p^{2}\exp(-c_{4}n)+2\epsilon, $$

where the maximum is taken with respect to the implicit index $i,j$ associated with $\delta$ and $\eta$ .

We now consider the term $v^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}\eta$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\max_{i,j\in[p]}|v^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}\eta| \displaystyle\leq\max_{i,j\in[p]}[v^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}v]^{1/2}[\eta^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}\eta]^{1/2} \displaystyle\leq\max_{i,j\in[p]}[|v^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}v-\Theta_{ii}|+|\Theta_{ii}|]^{1/2}[\eta^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}\eta]^{1/2} \displaystyle\leq[\max_{i\in[p]}|v^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}v-\Theta_{ii}|+\max_{i\in[p]}|\Theta_{ii}|]^{1/2}\max_{j\in[p]}[\eta^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}\eta]^{1/2}. $$

Under Assumption 4.1 (2), $\max_{i\in[p]}|\Theta_{ii}|$ is upper bounded. Combining the inequalities in Equation (132) and Equation (137), we have

$$ \mathbbm{P}\left(\max_{i,j\in[p]}|v^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}\eta|\geq\frac{c}{\sqrt{\log p}}\right)\leq 2p^{2}\exp\left(-c_{2}\frac{n}{\log p}\right)+2p^{2}\exp(-c_{4}n)+\epsilon. $$

The decomposition in Equation (128), along with the inequalities in Equation (132), Equation (137) and Equation (139) together imply the claim in Lemma A.14.

#### Corollary A.3.

The high probability bound in Lemma A.14 also applies to the normalized versions $\Lambda^{0}$ and $\Theta^{0}$ . That is, under Assumption 4.1, for any $\epsilon>0$ , there exist constants $c_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4}>0$ such that for large enough $n$ ,

$$ \mathbbm{P}\left(\max_{i,j\in[p]}\left|\Lambda^{0}_{ij}-\Theta^{0}_{ij}\right|\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{\log p}}\right)\geq 1-c_{1}p^{2}\exp\left(-c_{2}\frac{n}{\log p}\right)-c_{3}p^{2}\exp\left(-c_{4}n\right)-\epsilon. $$

Proof of Corollary A.3. We show that $\max_{i,j\in[p]}\left|\Lambda^{0}_{ij}-\Theta^{0}_{ij}\right|\leq c/\sqrt{\log p}$ for some constant $c>0$ , conditioning on the high probability event $\left\{\max_{i,j\in[p]}\left|\Lambda_{ij}-\Theta_{ij}\right|\leq{1}/{\sqrt{\log p}}\right\}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\max_{i,j\in[p]}\left|\Lambda^{0}_{ij}-\Theta^{0}_{ij}\right| \displaystyle=\max_{i,j\in[p]}\left|\frac{\Lambda_{ij}}{\sqrt{\Lambda_{ii}\Lambda_{jj}}}-\frac{\Theta_{ij}}{\sqrt{\Theta_{ii}\Theta_{jj}}}\right| \displaystyle\leq\max_{i,j\in[p]}\left|\frac{\Lambda_{ij}}{\sqrt{\Lambda_{ii}\Lambda_{jj}}}-\frac{\Lambda_{ij}}{\sqrt{\Theta_{ii}\Theta_{jj}}}\right|+\max_{i,j\in[p]}\left|\frac{\Lambda_{ij}}{\sqrt{\Theta_{ii}\Theta_{jj}}}-\frac{\Theta_{ij}}{\sqrt{\Theta_{ii}\Theta_{jj}}}\right|. $$

Consider the first term. By Assumption 4.1 (2), for large enough $p$ , we have

$$ \frac{|\Lambda_{ij}|}{\sqrt{\Lambda_{ii}\Lambda_{jj}}}\leq\frac{|\Lambda_{ij}-\Theta_{ij}|+\Theta_{ij}}{\sqrt{[\Theta_{ii}-|\Lambda_{ii}-\Theta_{ii}|][\Theta_{jj}-|\Lambda_{jj}-\Theta_{jj}|]}}\leq K $$

for some constant $K>0$ . It follows that

$$ \displaystyle\left|\frac{\Lambda_{ij}}{\sqrt{\Lambda_{ii}\Lambda_{jj}}}-\frac{\Lambda_{ij}}{\sqrt{\Theta_{ii}\Theta_{jj}}}\right| \displaystyle=\frac{|\Lambda_{ij}|}{\sqrt{\Lambda_{ii}\Lambda_{jj}}}\left|\left({\frac{\Lambda_{ii}\Lambda_{jj}}{\Theta_{ii}\Theta_{jj}}}\right)^{1/2}-1\right|\leq K\left|\left({\frac{\Lambda_{ii}\Lambda_{jj}}{\Theta_{ii}\Theta_{jj}}}\right)^{1/2}-1\right| \displaystyle\leq K\left|\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{\log p}\Theta_{ii}}\right)^{1/2}\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{\log p}\Theta_{jj}}\right)^{1/2}-1\right| \displaystyle\leq K\left|1+\frac{2C}{\sqrt{\log p}}+\frac{C^{2}}{\log p}-1\right|\leq\frac{K^{\prime}}{\sqrt{\log p}} $$

for some constant $K^{\prime}>0$ . In the last to second inequality above, we use an elementary inequality $\sqrt{1+x}\leq 1+x$ for $x>0$ .

For the second term, by Assumption 4.1 (2), we have

$$ \left|\frac{\Lambda_{ij}}{\sqrt{\Theta_{ii}\Theta_{jj}}}-\frac{\Theta_{ij}}{\sqrt{\Theta_{ii}\Theta_{jj}}}\right|\leq C{|\Lambda_{ij}-\Theta_{ij}|}\leq\frac{C}{\sqrt{\log p}}. $$

We note that both the upper bounds in Equation (143) and Equation (144) do not depend on the indexes $i,j$ . Therefore, we have shown that $\max_{i,j\in[p]}\left|\Lambda^{0}_{ij}-\Theta^{0}_{ij}\right|\leq(K^{\prime}+C)/\sqrt{\log p}$ . This implies the claim in Corollary A.3.

#### Lemma A.15.

Under Assumption 4.1, as $n,p\to\infty$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R},\ j\in S_{0}}\left|\mathbbm{P}(T_{j}>t)-Q(t)\right|\longrightarrow 0. $$

Proof of Lemma A.15. Recall that

$$ T_{j}={\sqrt{n}\widehat{\beta}_{j}^{d}}/{{\Lambda^{1/2}_{jj}}}\ \ \ \text{and}\ \ \ \widetilde{Z}_{j}:={Z_{j}}/{{\Lambda^{1/2}_{jj}}}\Big|X\sim N(0,1). $$

Without changing the selection result obtained via Algorithm 1, we multiply the normalized debiased Lasso estimator $T_{j}$ defined in Equation (23) by a constant factor $\sqrt{n}$ so that it follows the standard normal distribution asymptotically.

By Lemma A.14, for large enough $n$ , we have $\min_{j\in[p]}\Lambda_{jj}\geq c$ for some constant $c>0$ with high probability. Henceforth we condition on this high probability event. Recall the decomposition in Equation (20), thus for $j\in S_{0}$ , i.e., $\beta^{\star}_{j}=0$ , we have $T_{j}=\widetilde{Z}_{j}+\Delta_{j}/{\Lambda^{1/2}_{jj}}$ . Let $\epsilon=p_{1}\log p/\sqrt{n}\rightarrow 0$ by Assumption 4.1 (1). For the bias term $\Delta$ , we have

$$ \mathbbm{P}\left(||\Delta||_{\infty}\geq\epsilon\sqrt{c}\right)\leq\epsilon $$

by Theorem 2.3 in Javanmard and Montanari, (2013). It follows that for any $t\in\mathbbm{R}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbbm{P}\left(T_{j}>t\right)-Q(t) \displaystyle=\mathbbm{P}\big(\widetilde{Z}_{j}>t-\Delta_{j}/{\Lambda^{1/2}_{jj}}\big)-Q(t) \displaystyle\leq\mathbbm{P}(\widetilde{Z}_{j}>t-\epsilon)+\mathbbm{P}\left(||\Delta||_{\infty}\geq\epsilon\sqrt{c}\right)-Q(t) \displaystyle\leq Q(t-\epsilon)-Q(t)+\epsilon \displaystyle\leq c_{1}\epsilon $$

for some constant $c_{1}>0$ , in which the last inequality follows from the simple fact that for any $t\in\mathbbm{R},\ \epsilon>0$ , we have

$$ Q(t-\epsilon)-Q(t)=\int_{t-\epsilon}^{t}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)dx\leq\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}. $$

Similarly, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbbm{P}\left(T_{j}>t\right)-Q(t) \displaystyle\geq\mathbbm{P}(\widetilde{Z}_{j}>t+\epsilon)\mathbbm{P}(||\Delta||_{\infty}<\epsilon\sqrt{c})-Q(t) \displaystyle\geq Q(t+\epsilon)(1-\epsilon)-Q(t) \displaystyle\geq-c_{2}\epsilon. $$

for some constant $c_{2}>0$ . Since the bounds in Equation (147) and Equation (149) are irrelevant to $t$ and the index $j$ , the claim in Lemma A.15 follows.

#### Lemma A.16.

Under Assumption 4.1, as $n,p\to\infty$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}\textnormal{Var}\bigg(\frac{1}{p_{0}}\sum_{j\in S_{0}}\mathbbm{1}(M_{j}>t)\bigg)\longrightarrow 0. $$

Proof of Lemma A.16. Denote the correlated set as $\Gamma=\{(i,j):i,j\in S_{0},\ \Theta_{ij}\neq 0\}$ , and the uncorrelated set as $\Gamma^{c}=\{(i,j):i,j\in S_{0},\ \Theta_{ij}=0\}$ . We have the following decomposition.

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}\textnormal{Var}\bigg(\frac{1}{p_{0}}\sum_{j\in S_{0}}\mathbbm{1}(M_{j}>t)\bigg) \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{p_{0}^{2}}\sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}\sum_{(i,j)\in\Gamma}\text{Cov}(\mathbbm{1}(M_{i}>t),\mathbbm{1}(M_{j}>t)) \displaystyle+\frac{1}{p_{0}^{2}}\sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}\sum_{(i,j)\in\Gamma^{c}}\text{Cov}(\mathbbm{1}(M_{i}>t),\mathbbm{1}(M_{j}>t)) \displaystyle\leq\frac{|\Gamma|}{p_{0}^{2}}+\sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R},(i,j)\in\Gamma^{c}}\left|\mathbbm{P}(M_{i}>t,M_{j}>t)-H^{2}(t)\right| \displaystyle+\sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R},(i,j)\in\Gamma^{c}}\left|\mathbbm{P}(M_{i}>t)\mathbbm{P}(M_{j}>t)-H^{2}(t)\right|. $$

By Assumption 4.1 (1), we have $|\Gamma|/p_{0}^{2}\leq p_{0}\sqrt{n}/(p_{0}^{2}\log p)\to 0$ . Further, by Lemma A.5, we have

$$ \sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R},i,j\in S_{0}}\left|\mathbbm{P}(M_{i}>t)\mathbbm{P}(M_{j}>t)-H^{2}(t)\right|\to 0. $$

Therefore, it is sufficient for us to show that

$$ \sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R},(i,j)\in\Gamma^{c}}\left|\mathbbm{P}(M_{i}>t,M_{j}>t)-H^{2}(t)\right|\rightarrow 0,\ \ \ \text{as}\ n,p\to\infty. $$

In the following, we condition on the high probability event $E_{1}\cap E_{2}\cap E_{3}$ , in which

$$ \displaystyle E_{1} \displaystyle=\Big\{\min_{j\in[p]}\Lambda^{(1)}_{jj}\geq c\Big\}\cap\Big\{\min_{j\in[p]}\Lambda^{(2)}_{jj}\geq c\Big\}, \displaystyle E_{2} \displaystyle=\Big\{\max_{i,j\in[p]}|\Lambda_{ij}^{0,(1)}-\Theta^{0}_{ij}|\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{\log p}}\Big\}\cap\Big\{\max_{i,j\in[p]}|\Lambda_{ij}^{0,(2)}-\Theta^{0}_{ij}|\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{\log p}}\Big\}, \displaystyle E_{3} \displaystyle=\Big\{||\Delta^{(1)}||_{\infty}\leq\epsilon\sqrt{c}\Big\}\cap\Big\{||\Delta^{(2)}||_{\infty}\leq\epsilon\sqrt{c}\Big\}. $$

The superscripts $(1),(2)$ reflects the data splitting step, and the corresponding random variables are defined on each part of the data. $c>0$ is some suitable constant (see Lemma A.14 and Assumption 4.1 (2)), and $\epsilon=p_{1}\log p/\sqrt{n}\rightarrow 0$ by Assumption 4.1 (1).

We consider the same decomposition as in Equation (89), and proceed to upper bound $I_{1}$ . Let $\rho=1/\sqrt{\log p}$ . Notice that for $(i,j)\in\Gamma^{c}$ , $\Theta^{0}_{ij}=0$ , thus we have

$$ \max_{(i,j)\in\Gamma^{c}}\big|\Lambda^{0,(1)}_{i,j}\big|\leq\rho\ \ \ \text{and}\ \ \ \max_{(i,j)\in\Gamma^{c}}\big|\Lambda^{0,(2)}_{i,j}\big|\leq\rho $$

once we condition on the high probability event $E_{2}$ . Let $\widetilde{Z}^{(1)}$ and $\widetilde{Z}^{(2)}$ be the normalized version (e.g. variance 1) of $Z^{(1)}$ and $Z^{(2)}$ (see Equation (20)), respectively, thus $\Lambda^{0,(1)}$ and $\Lambda^{0,(2)}$ are essentially the corresponding covariance matrices. We have

$$ \displaystyle I_{1} \displaystyle\leq\mathbbm{P}\left(\widetilde{Z}_{i}^{(2)}>I_{t}\big(T_{i}^{(1)}\big)-\epsilon,\widetilde{Z}_{j}^{(2)}>I_{t}\big(T_{j}^{(1)}\big)-\epsilon,T_{i}^{(1)}>0,T_{j}^{(1)}>0\right) \displaystyle=\mathbbm{E}\left[\mathbbm{P}\big(\widetilde{Z}_{i}^{(2)}>I_{t}(x)-\epsilon,\widetilde{Z}_{j}^{(2)}>I_{t}(y)-\epsilon\big)\mid T_{i}^{(1)}=x>0,\ T_{j}^{(1)}=y>0\right] \displaystyle\leq c_{1}\rho+\mathbbm{E}\left[Q\big(I_{t}(x)-\epsilon\big)Q\big(I_{t}(y)-\epsilon\big)\mid T_{i}^{(1)}=x>0,\ T_{j}^{(1)}=y>0\right] \displaystyle\leq c_{1}\rho+c_{2}\epsilon+\mathbbm{E}\left[Q\big(I_{t}(x)\big)Q\big(I_{t}(y)\big)\mid T_{i}^{(1)}=x>0,\ T_{j}^{(1)}=y>0\right] $$

for some constants $c_{1},c_{2}>0$ , in which the third line is based on the Mehler’s identity (see Equation (90)) and Lemma 1 in Azriel and Schwartzman, (2015), and the last line is based on the inequality in Equation (148). Similarly, we can upper bound $I_{2}$ , $I_{3}$ and $I_{4}$ . Combining the four upper bounds together, we obtain an upper bound on $\mathbbm{P}(M_{i}>t,M_{j}>t)$ specified as below,

$$ \mathbbm{P}\left(\text{sign}(W_{i}^{(2)}T_{i}^{(1)})f(W_{i}^{(2)},T_{i}^{(1)})>t,\text{sign}(W_{j}^{(2)}T_{j}^{(1)})f(W_{j}^{(2)},T_{j}^{(1)})>t\right)+4c_{1}\rho+4c_{2}\epsilon, $$

in which $W_{i}^{(2)}$ and $W_{j}^{(2)}$ are two independent random variables (also independent to everything else) following the standard normal distribution. We can further decompose the first term in Equation (156) into four terms as Equation (89) by conditioning on the signs of $W_{i}^{(2)}$ and $W_{j}^{(2)}$ , and repeat the upper bound in Equation (155). This leads to

$$ \mathbbm{P}(M_{i}>t,M_{j}>t)\leq H^{2}(t)+8c_{1}\rho+8c_{2}\epsilon. $$

Similarly, we can establish the corresponding lower bound. Thus we complete the proof of Lemma A.16.

#### A.6.2 Proof of Proposition 4.1

In addition to the notations introduced in Section A.3.2, we denote

$$ \displaystyle G^{0}_{p}(t)=\frac{1}{p_{0}}\sum_{j\in S_{0}}\mathbbm{P}(M_{j}>t),\ \ \ V^{0}_{p}(t)=\frac{1}{p_{0}}\sum_{j\in S_{0}}\mathbbm{P}(M_{j}<-t). $$

The proof of Proposition 4.1 is essentially the same as the proof of Proposition 3.2, with the help of the following Lemma A.17.

#### Lemma A.17.

Under Assumption 4.1, as $n,p\to\infty$ , we have in probability,

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}\left|\widehat{G}^{0}_{p}(t)-H(t)\right|\longrightarrow 0, \displaystyle\sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}\left|\widehat{V}^{0}_{p}(t)-H(t)\right|\longrightarrow 0. $$

Proof of Lemma A.17. We prove the first claim. The second claim follows similarly. Notice that $H(t)$ is symmetric about 0. By Lemma A.5, it is sufficient for us to show that

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}\left|\widehat{G}^{0}_{p}(t)-G^{0}_{p}(t)\right|\longrightarrow 0, \displaystyle\sup_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}\left|\widehat{V}^{0}_{p}(t)-V^{0}_{p}(t)\right|\longrightarrow 0. $$

The proof follows similarly as the proof of Lemma A.8 using an $\epsilon$ -net argument, except that we use the Chebyshev’s inequality and Lemma A.16 in Equation (102).

### A.7 Proof of Proposition 4.2 and 4.3

Without loss of generality, we assume that the Lipschitz constant of $\ddot{\rho}(v)$ is 1 (see Assumption 4.2 (3)). For $j\in[p]$ , denote $\eta_{j}=X_{\beta^{\star},j}-X_{\beta^{\star},-j}\gamma_{j}$ , and denote $\tau_{j}^{2}=\mathbbm{E}[\eta_{j}^{\top}\eta_{j}/n]$ as the conditional variance $\text{Var}(X_{\beta^{\star},j}|X_{\beta^{\star},-j})$ . Denote $\widehat{\Sigma}=P_{n}\dot{\ell}_{\widehat{\beta}}\dot{\ell}^{\top}_{\widehat{\beta}}$ as the sample version of $\Sigma$ .

#### A.7.1 Technical lemmas

#### Lemma A.18.

Under Assumption 4.2, for any $\epsilon>0$ , there exists a constant $C_{\epsilon}>0$ , such that $\mathbbm{P}(\cap_{i=1}^{4}E^{\epsilon}_{i})\geq 1-\epsilon$ , in which the events $E^{\epsilon}_{1},E^{\epsilon}_{2},E^{\epsilon}_{3},E^{\epsilon}_{4}$ are defined as below,

$$ \displaystyle E^{\epsilon}_{1}=\left\{\frac{1}{n}||X(\widehat{\beta}-\beta^{\star})||_{2}^{2}\leq C_{\epsilon}p_{1}\log p/n\right\}, \displaystyle E^{\epsilon}_{2}=\left\{||\widehat{\beta}-\beta^{\star}||_{1}\leq C_{\epsilon}p_{1}\sqrt{\log p/n}\right\}, \displaystyle E^{\epsilon}_{3}=\left\{\max_{j\in[p]}||\widehat{\gamma}_{j}-\gamma_{j}||_{1}\leq C_{\epsilon}s\sqrt{\log p/n}\right\}, \displaystyle E^{\epsilon}_{4}=\left\{\max_{j\in[p]}||\widehat{\gamma}_{j}-\gamma_{j}||_{2}\leq C_{\epsilon}\sqrt{s\log p/n}\right\}. $$

Proof of Lemma A.18. Lemma A.18 follows from standard arguments in Bickel et al., (2009), Raskutti et al., (2010), Bühlmann and Van de Geer, (2011), Van de Geer et al., (2014).

#### Lemma A.19.

Under Assumption 4.2, we have

$$ \displaystyle\max_{j\in[p]}\left|\widehat{\tau}_{j}^{2}-\tau_{j}^{2}\right|=O_{p}\big(\sqrt{s\log p/n}\big), \displaystyle\max_{j\in[p]}\left|{1}/{\widehat{\tau}_{j}^{2}}-{1}/{\tau_{j}^{2}}\right|=O_{p}\big(\sqrt{s\log p/n}\big). $$

Proof of Lemma A.19. The proof follows similarly as the proof of Theorem 3.2 in Van de Geer et al., (2014), combined with some enriched arguments that we detail below. For any $\epsilon>0$ , we condition on the high probability event $\cap_{i=1}^{4}E^{\epsilon}_{i}$ . Since $X_{\widehat{\beta}}=W_{\widehat{\beta}}W_{\beta^{\star}}^{-1}X_{\beta^{\star}}$ , we have the following decomposition,

$$ \widehat{\tau}^{2}_{j}-\tau_{j}^{2}=\frac{1}{n}X_{\widehat{\beta},j}^{\top}\left(X_{\widehat{\beta},j}-X_{\widehat{\beta},-j}\widehat{\gamma}_{j}\right)-\tau_{j}^{2}:=I_{1}+I_{2}, $$

in which

$$ \displaystyle I_{1} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}X_{\beta^{\star},j}^{\top}\left(X_{\beta^{\star},j}-X_{\beta^{\star},-j}\widehat{\gamma}_{j}\right)-\tau_{j}^{2}, \displaystyle I_{2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}X_{\beta^{\star},j}^{\top}\left(W^{2}_{\widehat{\beta}}W_{\beta^{\star}}^{-2}-I\right)\left(X_{\beta^{\star},j}-X_{\beta^{\star},-j}\widehat{\gamma}_{j}\right). $$

We proceed to upper bound $I_{1}$ and $I_{2}$ .

We further decompose $I_{1}$ into four terms, $I_{1}=I_{11}+I_{12}+I_{13}+I_{14}$ , in which

$$ \displaystyle I_{11} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\eta_{i}^{\top}\eta_{j}-\tau_{j}^{2}, \displaystyle I_{12} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\eta_{j}^{\top}X_{\beta^{\star},-j}(\gamma_{j}-\widehat{\gamma}_{j}), \displaystyle I_{13} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\gamma_{j}^{\top}X_{\widehat{\beta},-j}^{\top}\left(X_{\widehat{\beta},j}-X_{\widehat{\beta},-j}\widehat{\gamma}_{j}\right), \displaystyle I_{14} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\gamma_{j}^{\top}X_{\beta^{\star},-j}^{\top}\left(I-W^{2}_{\widehat{\beta}}W_{\beta^{\star}}^{-2}\right)\left(X_{\beta^{\star},j}-X_{\beta^{\star},-j}\widehat{\gamma}_{j}\right). $$

For $I_{11}$ , by Assumption 4.2 (2), we have

$$ ||\eta_{j}||_{\infty}\leq||X_{\beta^{\star},j}||_{\infty}+||X_{\beta^{\star},-j}\gamma_{j}||_{\infty}\leq 2C_{1}. $$

Since $\mathbbm{E}[\eta_{j}^{\top}\eta_{j}/n]=\tau_{j}^{2}$ , we have

$$ \max_{j\in[p]}I_{11}=O_{p}(\sqrt{\log p/n}), $$

based on the union bound and the Hoeffding’s inequality.

For $I_{12}$ , since $\mathbbm{E}[\eta_{j}^{\top}X_{\beta^{\star},-j}]=0$ , we have

$$ \max_{j\in[p]}||\eta_{j}^{\top}X_{\beta^{\star},-j}/n||_{\infty}=O_{p}(\sqrt{\log p/n}), $$

by the union bound and the Hoeffding’s inequality. It follows that

$$ \displaystyle\max_{j\in[p]}I_{12} \displaystyle\leq\max_{j\in[p]}||\eta_{j}^{\top}X_{\widehat{\beta},-j}/n||_{\infty}\max_{j\in[p]}||\widehat{\gamma}_{j}-\gamma_{j}||_{1} \displaystyle=O_{p}(s\log p/n). $$

For $I_{13}$ , since $\gamma_{j}$ is $s-$ sparse, by Assumption 4.2 (2), we have

$$ \displaystyle\max_{j\in[p]}||\gamma_{j}||_{1} \displaystyle\leq\sqrt{s}\max_{j\in[p]}||\gamma_{j}||_{2} \displaystyle=\sqrt{s}\max_{j\in[p]}[\Sigma_{j,-j}\Sigma_{-j,-j}^{-2}\Sigma_{-j,j}]^{1/2} \displaystyle\leq\sqrt{s}C_{1}^{2}/C_{2}. $$

In addition, by the KKT condition of the $j$ -th nodewise Lasso regression, we have

$$ \max_{j\in[p]}||X_{\widehat{\beta},-j}^{\top}\left(X_{\widehat{\beta},j}-X_{\widehat{\beta},-j}\widehat{\gamma}_{j}\right)/n||_{\infty}\leq\lambda_{j}. $$

It follows that

$$ \displaystyle\max_{j\in[p]}I_{13} \displaystyle\leq\max_{j\in[p]}||\gamma_{j}||_{1}\max_{j\in[p]}||X_{\widehat{\beta},-j}^{\top}\left(X_{\widehat{\beta},j}-X_{\widehat{\beta},-j}\widehat{\gamma}_{j}\right)/n||_{\infty} \displaystyle=O_{p}(\sqrt{s\log p/n}). $$

For $I_{14}$ , we first notice that

$$ \displaystyle||X_{\beta^{\star},j}-X_{\beta^{\star},-j}\widehat{\gamma}_{j}||_{\infty} \displaystyle\leq||\eta_{j}||_{\infty}+||X_{\beta^{\star},-j}(\gamma_{j}-\widehat{\gamma}_{j})||_{\infty} \displaystyle\leq 2C_{1}+C_{1}||\gamma_{j}-\widehat{\gamma}_{j}||_{1} \displaystyle\leq 3C_{1} $$

by Assumption 4.2 (2) and Equation (166). By Assumption 4.2 (3), it follows that

$$ \displaystyle\max_{j\in[p]}I_{14} \displaystyle\leq\frac{3C_{1}^{2}}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\frac{\ddot{\rho}(x_{i}^{\intercal}\widehat{\beta})-\ddot{\rho}(x_{i}^{\intercal}\beta^{\star})}{\ddot{\rho}(x_{i}^{\intercal}\beta^{\star})}\right| \displaystyle=O_{p}(||X(\widehat{\beta}-\beta^{\star})||_{2}/\sqrt{n}) \displaystyle=O_{p}(\sqrt{p_{1}\log p/n}), $$

in which the second inequality follows from Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Combining the upper bound on $\max_{j\in[p]}I_{11}$ , $\max_{j\in[p]}I_{12}$ , $\max_{j\in[p]}I_{13}$ and $\max_{j\in[p]}I_{14}$ , we show that

$$ \max_{j\in[p]}I_{1}=O_{p}(\sqrt{s\log p/n}). $$

Finally, $\max_{j\in[p]}I_{2}$ can be upper bounded similarly as $\max_{j\in[p]}I_{14}$ . This completes the proof of the first claim in Lemma A.19. The second claim follows by noticing that $1/\tau_{j}^{2}$ is uniformly upper bounded because

$$ 1/\tau_{j}^{2}=\Theta_{j,j}\leq\sigma_{\max}(\Theta)=1/\sigma_{\min}(\Sigma)\leq C_{2}. $$

This completes the proof of Lemma A.19

#### Lemma A.20.

Under Assumption 4.2, we have

$$ \displaystyle\max_{j\in[p]}||\widehat{\Theta}_{j,\cdot}-\Theta_{j,\cdot}||_{1}=O_{p}(s\sqrt{\log p/n}), \displaystyle\max_{j\in[p]}||\widehat{\Theta}_{j,\cdot}-\Theta_{j,\cdot}||_{2}=O_{p}(\sqrt{s\log p/n}), \displaystyle\max_{j\in[p]}|\widehat{\Theta}_{j,\cdot}\Sigma\widehat{\Theta}_{j,\cdot}^{\top}-\Theta_{j,j}|=O_{p}(\sqrt{s\log p/n}). $$

Proof of Lemma A.20. By Lemma A.18 and A.19, for any $\epsilon>0$ , there exists a constant $C_{\epsilon}>0$ , such that $\mathbbm{P}(\cap_{i=1}^{6}E^{\epsilon}_{i})\geq 1-\epsilon$ , in which $E_{i}^{\epsilon}$ for $i\in[4]$ are specified in Lemma A.18, and

$$ \displaystyle E_{5}^{\epsilon}=\left\{\max_{j\in[p]}\left|\widehat{\tau}_{j}^{2}-\tau_{j}^{2}\right|\leq C_{\epsilon}\sqrt{s\log p/n}\right\}, \displaystyle E_{6}^{\epsilon}=\left\{\max_{j\in[p]}\left|1/\widehat{\tau}_{j}^{2}-1/\tau_{j}^{2}\right|\leq C_{\epsilon}\sqrt{s\log p/n}\right\}. $$

We first note that by Equation (176),

$$ 1/\widehat{\tau}_{j}^{2}\leq|1/\widehat{\tau}_{j}^{2}-1/\tau_{j}^{2}|+1/\tau_{j}^{2}\leq 2C_{2}. $$

Thus, by Equation (170), we have

The proof of Proposition 4.3 essentially follows the same as the proof of Proposition 4.1.
